articles.title: What is ranked-choice voting and how does it work in US elections?
articles.summary: Ranked-choice voting in Alaska could shape a key 2026 race, amid a US lawsuit involving two candidates named Dan Sullivan.
articles.body:
In Alaska, a controversy is unfolding over whether two Senate candidates with roughly the same name will cancel each other out.

The debate has shone a spotlight on a relatively uncommon style of voting in the United States: a system known as “ranked choice”.

Only two states in the United States — Alaska and Maine — employ ranked-choice voting throughout their territory, though major cities like New York have also embraced the practice.

Ranked-choice ballots allow voters to rank candidates in order of preference, rather than choosing just one. If a voter’s first choice does not win a majority, their vote can be transferred to their second pick.

With US midterm elections set for November 3, ranked-choice voting could play a role in closely watched races, including the Alaska Senate battle.

Here’s a guide on how ranked-choice voting works in the US:

What are the benefits of ranked-choice voting?

Proponents of ranked-choice voting believe the practice frees voters from the pressure of having to vote pragmatically. They no longer have to cast their ballot based on the candidate most likely to win.

Instead, supporters say that ranked-choice voting allows people to support the candidate they prefer the most, without the fear of “wasting” their vote should that candidate prove to be unpopular.

Advocates for ranked-choice voting also argue that the system reduces the spoiler effect, whereby a third-party or lesser-known candidate draws votes from a similar major-party candidate.

They also frame the system as a boon for democracy, by encouraging more diverse viewpoints to compete in elections and offering an incentive for candidates to work together.

Critics argue that ranked-choice ballots make voting and vote-counting more complicated.

They also fear it could slow down the tallying of election results, undermining confidence in the outcome.

A 2025 study published in the journal Political Behavior cited data suggesting that 4.8 percent of ranked-choice ballots are “improperly marked” — though it clarified that not all of those ballots are invalidated as a result.

On a ranked-choice ballot, voters get to number their candidates in order of preference. If their first choice doesn’t win, their vote automatically counts for their next choice instead.

If one candidate receives more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, that candidate wins.

If no candidate secures a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Ballots for that candidate are redistributed to voters’ next-ranked choices, and the votes are tallied again.

This continues until a candidate wins a majority of votes still counted in the final round.

If a voter ranks only one candidate and that candidate is eliminated, their ballot cannot transfer to another candidate.

Unlike a traditional runoff election, which requires voters to return to the polls, ranked-choice voting can determine a winner through successive rounds of counting in a single election.

Why do Alaska and Maine use ranked-choice voting?

Maine adopted ranked-choice voting in 2016 after concerns emerged about candidates winning elections without majority support. It first used the system in congressional elections in 2018.

Alaska voters approved the system through a 2020 ballot initiative. The state uses open primaries in which all candidates compete, with the top four advancing to a general election decided by ranked-choice voting.

Will ranked-choice voting affect Alaska’s Senate race?

Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system could come under scrutiny in this year’s Senate race, where two candidates named Dan Sullivan appear on the ballot.

The potential for voter confusion raises questions about whether some voters could accidentally rank the wrong candidate, potentially affecting how votes are distributed in successive rounds of ballot-counting.

State officials have taken steps to differentiate the two Sullivans on the ballot.

The incumbent, Senator Dan S Sullivan, is listed as a registered Republican and the incumbent, while his challenger, retired teacher Daniel J Sullivan Jr, has no party identification next to his name.

Still, the teacher’s inclusion has been the source of ongoing controversy, particularly in the wake of a New York Times report signalling he may have been recruited by Democrats as a spoiler candidate.

Republicans have raised concerns that having two Sullivans on the ballot could confuse voters and draw support away from the senator.

The teacher, meanwhile, has said his candidacy is genuine. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court allowed the vote to proceed with the participation of both Sullivans.

But the controversy has prompted US President Donald Trump to sue Alaska , seeking to block certification of the Senate election results if the incumbent Dan S Sullivan loses.

The lawsuit argues that confusion over the two candidates’ names could affect the outcome, but Alaska officials and Democrats are challenging the case.

Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states, and the lawsuit has raised concerns that the federal government might seek to meddle in Alaska’s vote count.

What other states have considered ranked-choice voting?

Ranked-choice voting is used in various local elections nationwide, including in New York City and San Francisco. Hawaii also uses it for certain special elections, while Washington, DC, adopted it for federal and local elections beginning in 2026.

Earlier this year, Virginia approved legislation expanding the use of ranked-choice voting.

But the system remains contested by some states. An estimated 19 states have laws prohibiting or restricting ranked-choice voting, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

articles.title: Peltola repeats denial of ballot-stacking reports, stays silent on federal probe
articles.summary: Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied once again any involvement in the alleged ballot-stacking scheme that it was recently reported her campaign engaged in during a rally on Friday, but did not mention the ongoing investigations into the scheme “I am so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s…
articles.body:
Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied once again any involvement in the alleged ballot-stacking scheme that it was recently reported her campaign engaged in during a rally on Friday, but did not mention the ongoing investigations into the scheme

“I am so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s candidacy,” Peltola said during h er speech at the rally. “Of course, I want fewer candidates in the primary. I’m not out soliciting more competition.”

“I do not need any help winning this race except by all of you in this room and the massive amounts of support we have across the state,” she added.

The high-stakes Senate race in Alaska has been consistently making the headlines after the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election, claiming the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could give Peltola an unfair advantage in the upcoming election.

The latest accusations stem from a recent New York Times report that said the Democrat’s campaign was directly involved in recruiting a man named Dan J. Sullivan in an effort to dilute votes. Several GOP lawmakers took to social media to blast the Peltola following the Times story.

Peltola has previously denied any knowledge or involvement in the alleged ballot-stacking scheme.

In the latest filing in its lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election, the DOJ accused Peltola of misleading a federal court . The amended complaint filed Thursday said Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee “orchestrated this sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected.”

The filing also cited the Times report saying, “although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief.”

The department also issued dozens of subpoenas in connection with the case, which have been sent to Peltola’s Senate campaign offices as well as the offices of Dan J. Sullivan.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) ordered an investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign violated state law in the alleged scheme. The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee also launched an investigation into Peltola’s campaign.

President Trump also accused Peltola of election fraud and said she should be removed from the ballot.

During her Friday’s speech, Peltola did not mention the investigations into the matter. She did, however, addressed the accusations calling them “hollow.”

“Our work isn’t done yet because we know that there are people out there who have not voted, who don’t have a plan to vote, who are who are so turned off by the smear campaigns and the garbage,” she said.

Scott Kendall, an Alaska lawyer and former GOP operative, told The Hill that even if Peltola’s campaign did indeed recruit Dan J. Sullivan, that action would not be against the law.

“It can be a nasty, dirty trick,” he said. “There can be bad motives behind it, but according to our Alaska Supreme Court, which is empowered to interpret Alaska law, it is not illegal.”

articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter
articles.summary: Ruling ‘with prejudice’ means US president may not amend or refile his lawsuit over his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein
articles.body:
A US judge dismissed Donald Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice on Saturday, according to a court filing, bringing an end to his legal challenge over the newspaper's reporting on his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein.

The decision follows an earlier dismissal in April that had allowed Trump to revise his complaint. As of Saturday, the case is dismissed with prejudice, meaning the lawsuit cannot be amended or refiled.

The case stemmed from a Wall Street Journal article alleging that Trump had sent a "bawdy" letter to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump denied the letter was real, insisting instead it had been fabricated.

Throughout the proceedings, the court repeatedly pointed to the newspaper's efforts to obtain Trump's response before publication and its inclusion of his direct denials as evidence that it had followed appropriate reporting standards.

Judge Darrin P Gayles issued the final dismissal on Saturday after determining that Trump's amended complaint still failed to establish "actual malice", the high legal threshold public figures must meet when pursuing defamation claims.

"As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed," the ruling said. "And because this is President Trump's second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate."

Trump, who has frequently pursued legal action against media organizations both during and outside his time in the White House, has maintained that the lewd drawing described in the Journal's report was fake.

A spokesperson for Trump's legal team shared a statement following the ruling: "President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."

A Dow Jones spokesperson said: "We're pleased with the court's decision."

Representatives for the Journal had asked the judge to dismiss the claim, arguing that the story was accurate and that it did not meet the bar for defamation. They argued that the reporters had neither knowingly published false information nor proceeded with the belief that the material was likely to be false.

The lawsuit attracted particular attention because it named Rupert Murdoch, one of Trump's most prominent media allies, among the defendants. Murdoch's News Corporation media empire owns the Journal. Before the article was published on 17 July 2025, Trump personally contacted Murdoch in an effort to stop its publication.

The report was published under the headline "Jeffrey Epstein's Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was From Donald Trump."

The Journal did not originally publish the image, though it was released by the House oversight committee in September after it was provided by Epstein's estate.

President Trump made a surprise reversal this week after his last-minute decision to cancel rallies in battleground states, announcing a day later he would travel to Kansas…
articles.body:
With just days to go before the midterm elections, Republicans and Democrats are making their final case to voters to turn out at the polls on Nov. 3.

President Trump made a surprise reversal this week after his last-minute decision to cancel rallies in battleground states, announcing a day later he would travel to Kansas and Iowa for events on Sunday after all.

Polling has shown tight Senate races for Republicans in these states, and in places like Michigan, Alaska, South Carolina, Georgia and Texas.

The candidates vying for Iowa’s open Senate seat — Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) — are scheduled to join CNN’s “Inside Politics Sunday” this weekend.

Additionally, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger (R) will join NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) will appear on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” this Sunday to discuss their respective gubernatorial races.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a nonpartisan election handicapper, places the Democratic Party’s odds of regaining control of the House at an 83 percent probability, according to a Saturday afternoon forecast . The chance the Democrats retake the Senate is around 63 percent, according to DDHQ .

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin will join “The Hill Sunday” this weekend to discuss how the party is approaching Election Day. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), the chair of the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), will appear on MS NOW’s “The Weekend” show.

articles.title: 5 state Supreme Court races to watch on Tuesday
articles.summary: Voters in half of the country will decide who sits on the bench of their state’s highest court next Tuesday. State Supreme Court races are on ballot in two dozen states this November, with partisan, nonpartisan and retention contests determining which candidates win seats or remain on the bench of courts that often have the final word…
articles.body:
Voters in half of the country will decide who sits on the bench of their state’s highest court next Tuesday.

State Supreme Court races are on ballot in two dozen states this November, with partisan, nonpartisan and retention contests determining which candidates win seats or remain on the bench of courts that often have the final word on interpreting state law in consequential matters like abortion and redistricting.

“State Supreme Court is a super important level of the ballot for us because so much of people’s rights and liberties is now determined at the state level,” said Deirdre Schifeling, the chief political and advocacy officer for the ACLU, which has spent about $5.5 million on voter outreach efforts in Michigan, Montana and North Carolina.

And while the ideological balance of power isn’t up for grabs in most states, experts say what happens next week could set the stage for shifts in 2028 and beyond.

Here are five races to watch on election night:

In Michigan, six candidates are running for two seats on the state’s Supreme Court.

Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh is seeking another eight-year term, and Justice Noah Hood is seeking his first full term. Hood was appointed to the high court by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) after former Chief Justice Elizabeth Clement retired in 2025.

All of the candidates will be placed on the same ballot, which also includes contenders Michael Warren, Casandra Morse-Bills, Thomas Howe and Jody White in an open election where the top two vote-getters will be declared winners.

The Wolverine State uses a unique method to determine which names make it on the general election ballot. Political parties select candidates during nominating conventions, but the elections are technically nonpartisan, so those party labels are not listed.

It’s no secret which way each candidate leans politically.

Cavanagh and Hood are Democratic Party nominees, while lower court judges Morse-Bills and Warren were nominated by Republicans.

Howe and White were both nominated by the U.S. Taxpayers Party, the state affiliate of the ultraconservative Constitution Party. The Michigan Advance reports that neither is licensed to practice law in Michigan, a requirement for any judge or justice in the state court system.

Recent election cycles have helped shore up liberals’ 6-1 advantage on the Michigan Supreme Court, with only one Republican-backed justice currently on the bench.

Both Democratic incumbents losing their reelection bids would tighten those margins but keep the majority intact.

A Democratic appointee in Missouri is running to keep his seat on the state’s high court — but he has no opponent.

Justice Paul Wilson, who was appointed to the Missouri Supreme Court bench in 2012, is facing a retention vote. That’s an up-and-down vote to decide whether an incumbent keeps their job.

There isn’t a power balance at stake, as justices appointed by Republican governors hold a 5-2 edge on the bench. But it remains to be seen whether a mid-decade redistricting fight that ran through the Supreme Court will have any bearing on voters.

Wilson authored the dissenting opinion in a narrow March decision that found the GOP-controlled legislature could redraw congressional lines before the next U.S. census.

In September he joined with colleagues on a unanimous decision that invalidated a 7-1 House map that sought to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) district and hand Republicans a pickup opportunity in the midterms. The court ruled that the new lines, which had been used for the primaries, could not be implemented until voters weighed in on a general election referendum.

The battle made to the U.S. Supreme Court three times, with the GOP losing each round.

The Missouri Judicial Performance Review Committee, an independent, statewide panel that evaluates the performance of judges for retention, has recommended that Wilson should be retained.

It is rare for judges to lose retention elections. Wilson earned 63 percent yes votes the last time he was on the ballot, according to state election results.

The race to replace a retiring justice on the Montana Supreme Court is a rematch between two lower court judges.

Flathead County judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are running to succeed outgoing Justice Beth Baker, who is stepping down after 16 years on the bench.

The pair have already faced each other once this year, with Eddy securing just over 7,600 more votes than Wilson in the June primary. As the only two candidates on the ballot, both advanced to the general election.

It’s officially a nonpartisan contest — meaning no party labels appear alongside their names — but that hasn’t stopped it from becoming something of a proxy battle.

The Montana GOP has lined up behind Wilson, hosting him as the keynote speaker at the state party’s winter kickoff event in February.

“I call myself a constitutional Conservative because I decide cases based on the facts and not feelings, principles above all else, and the Constitution,” Wilson said at the time, according to Montana Public Radio .

Eddy, meanwhile, has picked up endorsements from labor unions and environmental groups like the Montana Conservation Voters.

“When Montana constitutionalised environmental protections, it did so with the understanding that courts would serve as a forum where those rights were taken seriously, interpreted faithfully, and enforced when necessary,” Eddy said in a statement shared by the group.

Outside groups have spent a combined roughly $2.25 million in the contest, according to TV advertising data compiled by the Brennan Center for Justice .

In addition to electing a state Supreme Court justice, voters are also weighing a ballot measure that would enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution after the GOP-controlled legislature tried unsuccessfully to advance bills that would have made them partisan.

“We believe that there is an effort underway in Montana at the state legislative level to make state supreme courts partisan as a way to eventually elect Republican, hard right judges who will then take away reproductive rights,” said Schifeling.

The court currently has a 4-3 liberal lean, though experts note that Baker has sometimes acted as a swing vote. That leaves room for a potential ideological flip if Wilson emerges on top.

The outcome could prove even more important in 2028, when two state Supreme Court seats will be up for election.

A lot of eyes — and money — is also on North Carolina, where Democratic incumbent Justice Anita Earls is defending her seat against former Republican state lawmaker Sarah Stevens.

It’s the only seat up for election on the state Supreme Court this Tuesday, but it’s one that both parties have their eyes on looking ahead to 2028.

Republicans won a majority on the Tar Heel State’s top court in the 2022 midterms and, within months, reversed the court’s own prior rulings that had struck down a voter ID law and redistricting maps as unconstitutional.

The 2022 results followed years of wrangling between the GOP and Democrats over how the state’s judicial elections should be held. Those races were partisan for much of the 20th century , but after Republicans started winning more in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Democratic lawmakers removed party labels from the ballot.

State Supreme Court elections remained that way until 2016, when the Republican-controlled legislature changed them back to partisan after liberals secured a one-seat majority.

The contests have largely fallen along the state’s broader political lines since then, and conservatives now have a 5-2 edge.

A win for Stevens would expand that advantage, while Democrats are hoping Earls can cling to her seat to avoid shrinking the minority even further. Democratic incumbent Allison Riggs barely won reelection two years ago in a hotly contested election by less than 1,000 votes.

Tuesday’s race has attracted millions of dollars, with figures from the Brennan Center showing Earls has spent just shy of $4.2 million. North Carolina Families First, a left-leaning PAC, also launched a multimillion advertising blitz targeting Stevens.

The implications for 2028 are potentially big. Three sitting Republican justices are up for election that cycle, and at least one has already said he won’t seek another term.

Five of the nine seats on the Washington Supreme Court are up for election.

Chief Justice Debra Stephens is facing attorney Todd Bloom in her bid for another six-year term. Stephens has been on the bench since 2008.

Justice Theo Angelis and Justice Colleen Melody, both of whom were tapped by Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) to fill vacancies on the court this year, are seeking to finish out the remainder of the terms. They are being challenged by retired Federal Way Municipal Court Judge Dave Larson and attorney Scott Edwards, respectively.

The remaining two races are for seats left open by justices who opted not to seek re-election. King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell is squaring off against appellate Judge Ian Birk for one of those seats, while Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens is running against King County Superior Judge Jaime Hawk for the other.

Experts aren’t anticipating a major ideological shift in this cycle, but the officially nonpartisan races are still attracting plenty of attention.

The state Republican Party is backing attorney Edwards, Larson and Bloom in their bids to unseat the sitting justices. It has also endorsed Stevens and O’Donnell for the open seats.

Various Democratic officials and left-leaning groups like Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates have signaled their support for the three incumbents, as well as Birk and Hawk.

But it’s not a clean partisan split. O’Donnell has also picked up endorsements from some Democrats, according to his campaign.

The interest comes as the court is expected to take up major issues in the coming months, according to the Washington State Standard , including reforms to bail bond policy and a challenge to the state’s new income tax on high earners.

An initiative to repeal the tax is also on the ballot.

articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit over Jeffrey Epstein birthday card story
articles.summary: A federal judge in Florida has tossed a revised version of President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit against The Wall Street Journal over a story about a birthday card he allegedly sent Jeffrey Epstein more than two decades ago.
articles.body: A federal judge in Florida has tossed a revised version of President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit against The Wall Street Journal over a story about a birthday card he allegedly sent Jeffrey Epstein more than two decades ago. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles found Trump’s amended suit suffered from the same fatal flaw as his first attempt — it fell far short of the high legal bar to show the paper had published the story with “actual malice.” “As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed. And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate,” the judge wrote. Trump first sued the paper last July, shortly after the Journal published a story about a birthday book that Ghislaine Maxwell had assembled for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003. The book appeared to include a card from Trump, who had been friends with Epstein around that time. The card contained a hand-drawn outline of a naked woman with what appeared to be Trump’s first name signed in the pubic area. It included a typewritten note depicting an imaginary conversation with Epstein, who would later be charged with sex trafficking. Trump denied having anything to do with the card, and his suit accused the paper of having made it up and that no such note existed. Epstein’s estate later released a copy of a card matching the Journal’s description. Trump and the White House maintain the document is a fake. Trump’s suit alleged the writers of the article “falsely represent as fact that President Trump drew the naked woman’s breasts and signed his name ‘Donald’ below her waist, ‘mimicking pubic hair,’” and that the article caused him “overwhelming financial and reputational harm.” Trump’s suit also criticized the paper for not publishing an image of the card in the initial story, saying that shows “no authentic letter or drawing exists” — even though the House Oversight Committee publicly released the card after getting it from the Epstein estate. The suit says the Journal should have known the story was bogus because Trump said it was not true. It also chided the paper for failing to interview Epstein co-conspirator Maxwell, who’s serving 20 years in prison on sex trafficking charges. The story said Journal reporters wrote her a letter asking for an interview and included a comment from her attorney. The paper’s attorneys argued that like the original suit, Trump’s revised suit came “nowhere close” to demonstrating the paper acted with actual malice, in which “the false statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.” Despite Trump’s claim the paper failed to properly investigate the card before publishing the story, “the Article itself established that the Journal not only investigated” but also “informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it,” the paper said in its motion to dismiss the suit. Further, the attorneys argued, alleging that someone sent another person a birthday card is not defamatory. “There is nothing inherently defamatory about sending a bawdy letter to a friend,” the attorneys wrote, and the article “emphasizes that the Birthday Book was created before Epstein was first arrested” and “makes clear that President Trump’s friendship with Epstein ended years before Epstein was charged with sex crimes.” The attorneys also contended the suit should be dismissed because the public release of the card shows the story was “substantially true.” In an interview last year with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Maxwell acknowledged assembling the birthday book but said she could not remember whether Trump contributed to it. The White House maintains the signature is not Trump’s and that it looks different from his distinctive full signature. Democrats compiled a number of documents where Trump signed just his first name over the year, and the signatures appear very similar to the one on the card.

articles.title: How House Democrats' 'deterrence message' on Trump jobs could backfire
articles.summary: Elissa Slotkin's warning to young Americans about joining Trump's administration could hand Republicans legal ammunition under Trump v. Mazars.
articles.body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin's warning to young Americans not to join the Trump administration could backfire by handing Trump officials legal ammunition to derail the investigations Democrats hope to launch if they retake Congress, a former federal prosecutor warned. The freshman Michigan Democrat said last month that she wants her party to pursue "signature cases" against officials who helped Trump, reasoning that it would discourage young Americans from considering jobs in his administration. "I want that deterrence message sent," Slotkin said during an Oct. 13 event at the University of Chicago, describing how young graduates might fear "buying myself a ton of problems" by joining the administration. But Abhishek Kambli, a former deputy associate attorney general in Trump's Justice Department, said Slotkin's remarks could backfire if Democrats retake either chamber of Congress in the midterm elections and gain greater control over congressional investigations. "If they just throw in boilerplate language that this is for legislative purpose, anyone challenging those subpoenas will have that entire record to demonstrate that it's anything but that," Kambli, a partner at Holtzman Vogel, told Fox News Digital. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY While Congress has broad authority to conduct investigations, subpoena witnesses and review government operations, the Supreme Court has ruled that lawmakers cannot use those powers solely to punish individuals. The Supreme Court confronted those limits in 2020, when House Democrats attempted to obtain Trump's personal financial records through congressional subpoenas. In Trump v. Mazars, the justices established a four-factor test requiring courts to examine whether Congress demonstrated a legitimate legislative need for the records, whether its requests were sufficiently narrow, whether the information could be obtained elsewhere and what burden the subpoenas would impose on the president. The court sent the dispute back to lower courts without ruling that the subpoenas satisfied those standards, leaving unresolved questions about how the framework would be applied. "So it's not enough just to tack on a legislative purpose," Kambli said, arguing that courts must look beyond Congress' stated reasons for an investigation to determine whether its demands are constitutionally justified. Democrats' public remarks could become evidence against them if future subpoenas are challenged, according to Kambli. SLOTKIN WANTS GOP PROSECUTIONS TO DETER YOUNG PEOPLE FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION JOBS "They don't have to bury their head in the sand," Kambli said of the courts. "I think they have to look at the facts of the case and look at it in terms of how they fits into the broader comments that they made." House Democrats are already laying the groundwork for investigations into Trump's family business dealings and potential conflicts of interest if they regain control of Congress. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., has also vowed to expand his investigation into donors funding Trump's White House ballroom if Democrats retake the Senate, But another constitutional law expert questioned whether Democrats' remarks would carry enough legal weight to undermine future congressional investigations. Michael Morley, a professor at Florida State University College of Law, said courts generally recognize that politicians bring partisan motivations to congressional investigations and would be reluctant to invalidate subpoenas merely because of provocative public remarks. "I don't think that the fact that there might be partisan motivations for a congressional investigation would ultimately be a valid basis for refusing to comply with a subpoena," Morley told Fox News Digital. "At the end of the day, a court is going to be very reluctant to conclude, based on one or more members' possible subjective motivations, that Congress lacks constitutional authority to investigate," Morley said. SLOTKIN'S VIRAL 'THREAT' TO CONSERVATIVES TAKES NEW TWIST AS STUDENT MOVES TO HOLD HER ACCOUNTABLE: 'SHOCKING' He also emphasized that Trump v. Mazars focused specifically on subpoenas for the president's personal records, arguing that applying the same heightened legal standards to subpoenas targeting other administration officials would be a stretch. But Morley said Slotkin's language could give judges pause when the legal basis for a subpoena is already uncertain. "It's bad atmospherics," he said, adding that such statements could make courts "marginally less likely" to resolve doubts in Democrats' favor. Slotkin has rejected accusations that she wants to target Americans merely for working for Republicans. She told CNN that she was talking about officials who break the law or misuse taxpayer dollars, calling the criticism "manufactured outrage." But Kambli warned the consequences could extend beyond whether Democratic subpoenas survive legal challenges, saying that investigations could inflict financial and reputational damage even without criminal charges. "There is the idea that the process is the punishment, and there is no doubt that some members of Congress intend to use the process to bankrupt people that can't afford legal representation," Kambli said. He also said that while Trump's Justice Department would be unlikely to prosecute administration officials over criminal contempt referrals from a Democratic-controlled Congress, that could change under a future Democratic administration. Morley also criticized the prospect of intimidating young government employees who may lack the resources to defend themselves. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That's just not how we want our political disputes to be handled," Morley said.

articles.title: Legal filing questions Trump’s claims of non-citizen voting in California
articles.summary: Data scientists find that many ‘likely non-citizens’ identified by the Trump administration were erroneously flagged.
articles.body:
A new court filing has cast further doubt on the accuracy of a list of “likely non-citizen” voters that the administration of United States President Donald Trump sent to the state of California ahead of the midterm elections.

On Saturday, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), an advocacy group, submitted an analysis to the court conducted by two data scientists from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

It found that more than four in every 10 names on the list were not on California’s voter rolls.

It also found that thousands of potentially eligible US citizens were incorrectly identified as ineligible to vote.

The Trump administration’s list, delivered to California in early October, had suggested that as many as 20,930 “likely non-citizens” were registered on the state’s voter rolls.

That list has formed the basis of a lawsuit, filed on October 15, that calls on California to sequester any ballots sent to those “likely non-citizens”, preventing them from being tallied as part of voting results.

The lawsuit is unfolding in the final days before Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

Trump has expressed fear that, if his Republican Party loses its majorities in the two chambers of Congress, he could be impeached.

The Republican leader also has a track record of spreading false information about elections, including that his defeat in the 2020 presidential race was the result of a “rigged” vote.

He has often targeted California in his criticism. The state – the most populous in the country – is considered a longtime left-wing stronghold. It will elect 52 seats to the 435-member House of Representatives in Tuesday’s elections.

Already, Trump has accused California of “cheating” in its June 2 primary elections, after several Republican candidates underperformed, including Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt.

Under the US Constitution’s Elections Clause, election administration falls solely to the states, though Congress may pass regulations governing voting.

Critics, including California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, have cited that fact in their rebuttal to Trump’s lawsuit.

All 50 states already prohibit non-citizen voting in federal elections and undertake measures to prevent voter fraud, which is considered exceedingly rare.

Other states that have received similar lists of “likely non-citizen” voters have also found significant errors in the Trump administration’s accounting. Nevada, for example, found that none of the names included on that list were non-citizen voters.

Such errors have raised concerns that eligible citizens would see their votes denied if the Trump administration wins its California lawsuit.

Still, the Trump administration has threatened state officials with prosecution over the potential for non-citizen voting.

It has also vigorously pursued its lawsuit through federal court. On Friday, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco rejected the complaint a second time , determining it unconstitutional.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the court majority wrote in its ruling.

In Saturday’s court filing, the data scientists from UCLA’s Voting Rights Project found that 8,880 names on the list were not listed anywhere in California’s current voter files, a proportion of 42 percent.

Many other names on the list were either confirmed as US citizens or may correspond to US citizens.

“This review proves, at least as a preponderance of the evidence, that demands of election officials under criminal and civil threats, endangers the voting rights of plaintiff CHIRLA’s members and clients,” the filing said.

It was co-signed by the Democratic candidate to succeed Newsom as governor, Xavier Becerra.

articles.title: Mike Rogers claims he’s ahead by 7 percent on ballots returned so far ‘by our models’
articles.summary: Michigan’s Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers claimed he is ahead by almost seven percent on early-returned ballots, contrary to recent polls which lean in favor of his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed. “We’re actually about seven percent ahead on voters that we believe are voting for us returning their ballots,” Rogers said during an appearance on…
articles.body:
Michigan’s Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers claimed he is ahead by almost seven percent on early-returned ballots, contrary to recent polls which lean in favor of his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed.

“We’re actually about seven percent ahead on voters that we believe are voting for us returning their ballots,” Rogers said during an appearance on Fox News . Before mentioning the numbers, Rogers said they are “by our models.”

Rogers did not provide any further evidence backing up his claim, which is out of step with recent polling on the race.

A recent poll from CNN on Thursday found 49 percent of respondents backed or leaned toward El-Sayed, while 42 percent toward Rogers. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ leans heavily in favor of El-Sayed, giving him a 74 percent chance of winning the Senate race.

El-Sayed has made headlines in the closing weekend of the campaign for a public spat with his former Democratic primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.). He asked her to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday after a disagreement between the two stemming from a political ad supporting El-Sayed’s campaign that appeared to blame Israel and Jews for rising costs of living.

During his appearance on Fox, Rogers mentioned the spat involving Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish, who said he would not support El-Sayed in the upcoming elections and accused the Democrat of using antisemitic language on the campaign trail. Following that Stevens noted that she is still backing El-Sayed saying “like a lot of households in America, we’re a household divided.”

Rogers has sought to capitalize on El-Sayed’s perceived struggles courting Jewish voters with the race expected to be close

“We have a massive number of Jewish Democrats who are openly … organizing to vote for us,” Rogers told Fox News.

articles.title: Hegseth fired Nancy Lacore from the Navy. Now he could help her get to Congress
articles.summary: Democratic candidates on the midterm campaign trail are zeroing in on Pete Hegseth's leadership. Could that help them win?
articles.body:
Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore was a year into her command of the Navy Reserve when she was fired by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth , one of roughly two dozen high-ranking military leaders he purged or forced into retirement .

Unemployed for the first time after 35 years of Navy service, Lacore decided to run for Congress as a Democrat in South Carolina's 1st District. Or, more precisely, she decided to run against Hegseth, using her campaign to fiercely criticize his management of the military and highlight his responsibility for the Iran war.

Hegseth has become the public face of President Donald Trump 's deeply unpopular war in the Middle East, which has defined the midterms. But a string of scandals during Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon have provided Democrats with ample fodder for attacks that go beyond criticism of the war.

Democrats across the country have repeatedly brought up Hegseth's use of Signal, the commercial messaging app, to discuss a sensitive military operation , his ill-fated push to livestream an execution and his fixation on troops' testosterone levels . Hegseth has also faced backlash for pushing his evangelical Christianity on the Pentagon, most recently creating an Office of Religious Affairs that reports directly to him.

In South Carolina, Lacore has discussed how her career was upended by the Pentagon's personnel purge, which critics have denounced for disproportionately targeting women and Black senior military officers.

It is a strategy that has turned Hegseth into a foil for Democrats on the campaign trail. Criticism of the Pentagon's leadership has particularly resonated with voters in Lacore's heavily Republican district, which Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024.

"People are just concerned about the injection of politics and religion into the military," Lacore said in an interview with USA TODAY. "People who know the military know there is no place for either of those. It weakens the fabric that makes our military strong."

According to the latest polls, Lacore is running neck-and-neck with Republican nominee Jenny Honeycutt. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan elections forecaster, recently shifted its race prediction to "toss up" after predicting a Republican victory all year.

Hegseth's various controversies and "the fact that he's the poster child for the war – which is going badly and has driven up gas prices – combine to make him a ripe target politically," said Jeffrey Liszt, a partner at Impact Research, a Democratic polling firm.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, said at a recent rally that a Democratic majority would "run Pete Hegseth out of town." Former President Barack Obama skewered Hegseth's focus on physical appearances at a campaign rally in Ohio . Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, said "Hegseth is unfit" to lead the Pentagon.

Hegseth and Trump have struggled to find an answer to the criticisms in the final days of the campaign. Trump on Oct. 29 slammed a Republican-led impeachment effort against Hegseth and said the Iran war will end "very soon," a comment he has repeated for nearly eight months.

Sean Parnell, chief Pentagon spokesperson, wrote in a statement that Hegseth's team is "​​solely focused on Peace Through Strength and ensuring our warfighters have everything they need to be successful."

Lacore's district, home to many retirees and U.S. service members, runs along the coast in South Carolina from Beaufort to Charleston.

Until recently, the seat was viewed as a GOP stronghold. Rep. Nancy Mace, the retiring Republican incumbent, handily won her last two elections, creating the perception that the district was out of reach for Democrats. Mace, a former Trump ally, opted to run for governor of South Carolina and lost in the Republican primary. Trump didn't endorse Mace after she split with the president over releasing the Jeffrey Epstein files.

John Moffett, a Democratic strategist based in South Carolina, said in an interview that the district is "very tough, but not unwinnable" for a Democrat in this political environment.

"If anybody can do it, then certainly Nancy Lacore can," he added.

Lacore, who served in the Navy for more than three decades, said that the story of her abrupt firing "has come up organically in almost every room." She said it has helped her connect with Republican veterans who have grown increasingly wary of Hegseth's leadership at the Pentagon.

While Lacore has emphasized affordability and fuel prices in conversations with voters, she said that Hegseth's "mishandling of the military" has become a more widespread concern in the final months of the campaign.

"People are frustrated, scared and tired over everything that's going on," she said. "Mostly, people want confidence. They want me to be able to tell them that it's OK, that once Hegseth is out of there our military will recover and rebound."

If Lacore manages to flip the district, Hegseth will be a significant part of the reason why.

"There's this certain irony that Hegseth may have inadvertently helped create one of the most formidable Democratic congressional candidates in South Carolina that we've seen in a very long time," Moffett said.

Lacore said the Pentagon chief should not hold his breath waiting for a thank-you card if she wins Nov. 3. She'd sooner vote to impeach him.

"I certainly think he's deserving" of impeachment, Lacore said. "But I'm hopeful that maybe it will all be taken care of before I even get there."

Democrats have pledged to seek oversight and accountability in the Pentagon if they return to the majority, but they may not need to wait until a new Congress is seated in January to vote for Hegseth's impeachment.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Sept. 15, accusing the Pentagon chief of violating the Constitution by continuing the war in Iran without congressional approval.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, skirted the potentially damaging vote on impeaching Hegseth in September by canceling the House of Representatives' last day of work and sending members home early for an eight-week recess ahead of the midterms.

The decision by Massie to launch the impeachment effort provided Democratic candidates with more ammunition to go after Hegseth and helped make their criticisms seem more credible to voters, according to Liszt.

"The impeachment of Hegseth started with Republicans and not with Democrats," he said. "That's part of the reason why he's an opportune target."

Democrats have made Hegseth a focus of their campaign rallies in battleground states that will determine control of Congress. In remarks at a rally in Ohio on Oct. 24, Obama accused the Pentagon chief of misplacing his priorities as the Trump administration struggles to end a war in the Middle East that has upended the global economy and left national average gas prices above $4 a gallon.

"He's very focused on important matters, like the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops, and live streaming executions because that's how he thinks you cultivate that manly, warrior spirit," Obama said. "How much time do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?"

The criticism has not only come from Democratic lawmakers. Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, recently called his vote to confirm Hegseth the "biggest regret of my career."

Trump defended Hegseth in remarks to reporters before traveling to a midterm rally in South Carolina on Oct. 29.

"He's doing a great job. He's a great warrior," Trump said. "I think he's the best at his job in many, many years and a lot of people agree with that."

Massie, however, has vowed to renew his push to impeach Hegseth if he is still leading the Pentagon when lawmakers return to Washington on Nov. 9. The effort would be met with broad support from Democrats and potentially even a handful of Republicans in Congress.

"Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth's impeachment. It's the honorable thing to do," Massie wrote on social media . "The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election."

articles.title: Scott Colom releases ‘Sinners’-themed campaign ad as Mississippi Senate race heats up
articles.summary: Mississippi’s Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a “Sinners”-themed campaign ad over Halloween weekend, days ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. The movie’s premise revolves around the twins…
articles.body:
Mississippi’s Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a “Sinners”-themed campaign ad over Halloween weekend, days ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

The ad, released on TikTok , pays homage to the Academy Award-winning movie set in the Mississippi Delta in 1932 starring Michael B. Jordan, who played twins in the movie.

The movie’s premise revolves around the twins returning to their hometown where they set up a temporary juke joint one evening, celebrating African American culture with music and dance. Their evening takes a dark turn when vampires try to attack the establishment drawn by the musical talent of a young performer.

The ad released by Colom, titled “Sinators,” shows the two men guarding a door as a blonde woman, who seems to be impersonating the Democrat’s opponent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), tries to enter saying “please let me in, just give me one more chance, please.”

The conversation between the men revolves around holding the woman off “until the sun rises on election day.”

“She’s been feeding off Mississippi for years,” one of the brothers said in the ad. Colom posted the video with a caption that read “Sinators. Happy Halloween! (this is a joke!).”

The Senate race in Mississippi has been growing increasingly competitive with nonpartisan election forecasters shifting their ratings of the race from solid Republican to likely Republican. Decision Desk HQ , however, leans heavily in favor of Hyde-Smith, giving her a 91 percent chance of winning the race.

Recently, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) dropped $500,000 in the race in support of Colom.

President Trump traveled to the deep red state on Monday to boost voter turnout for the incumbent senator.

articles.title: Entenda como apoio a Flávio aumentou desafio de ACM Neto na Bahia | G1
articles.standfirst: Cientistas políticos preveem caminho difícil para representante do União Brasil no caso de uma nova candidatura em 2030.
articles.summary: Cientistas políticos preveem caminho difícil para representante do União Brasil no caso de uma nova candidatura em 2030
articles.body:
O apoio de ACM Neto ( União Brasil ) a Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) no segundo turno das eleições de 2026 aumentou o desafio do ex-prefeito de Salvador para ampliar a força da oposição ao PT na Bahia, estado que é governado pelo Partido dos Trabalhadores há 20 anos.

É o que apontam cientistas políticos após análise do resultado da votação e do cenário no estado, com as reeleições de Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT-BA) e Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), que manteve larga vantagem com o eleitorado baiano .

Mesmo com o aceno de Neto, que tinha se mantido neutro no primeiro turno, Flávio Bolsonaro não teve ganhos eleitorais relevantes nem em nível estadual e nem nas cidades onde já havia vencido. Ele conquistou apenas 166.176 votos a mais, um avanço de 28,53% para 28,69% entre um turno e outro. Lula, por outro lado, conquistou mais 820.487 votos, saltando de 66,17% para 71,31% dos votos válidos no 2º turno.

"Ao apoiar o adversário direto de Lula, ele [ACM Neto] reforça a imagem de antilulista que vinha tentando evitar. A reputação de um político se forma com sinais acumulados, e esse é um sinal forte, difícil de apagar até 2030", destacou, em entrevista ao g1 , o cientista político Ariel Calmon, coordenador de Análise Política Subnacional da BMJ.

Entenda como apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro aumenta desafio de ACM Neto para ampliar força da oposição ao PT na Bahia — Foto: Divulgação

📊 1º turno: 2.442.585 (28,53%) 📊 2º turno: 2.608.761 (28,69%)

📍 Buerarema 📊 1º turno: 4.796 (51,69%) 📊 2º turno: 5.037 (52,26%)

📍 Itamaraju 📊 1º turno: 17.365 (51,67%) 📊 2º turno: 18.322 (51,56%)

📍 Teixeira de Freitas 📊 1º turno: 38.670 (49,51%) 📊 2º turno: 41.454 (50,06%)

📍 Luís Eduardo Magalhães 📊 1º turno: 38.496 (62,03%) 📊 2º turno: 39.688 (61,6%)

Por outro lado, segundo o especialista, a decisão reforça no representante do União Brasil uma identidade mais nítida e o coloca como referência do campo anti-PT no estado — um eleitorado concentrado nas cidades grandes e que, na avaliação do estudioso, não tem outro líder de peso.

"O custo tende a ser menor em Salvador e na região metropolitana, onde a base dele já é mais oposicionista, e maior no interior, que é exatamente onde ele precisa crescer. Para 2028 [quando acontecem as eleições municipais], em Salvador, o impacto deve ser limitado. Já para uma nova disputa estadual, o caminho fica mais estreito", opinou Ariel Calmon.

Para Cláudio André Souza, professor de Ciência Política na Universidade da Integração Internacional da Lusofonia Afro-Brasileira (Unilab), a decisão poderia ser uma estratégia de sobrevivência que ACM Neto escolheu para encarar o ano de 2027, caso o candidato defendido por ele no 2º turno fosse eleito . Nesse caso, o risco não seria à toa. Em uma eventual vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro, Neto buscaria um cargo de primeiro ou segundo escalão em Brasília.

Mas também enfrentaria outro obstáculo nesse cenário que não se concretizou: disputar espaço como uma liderança no nordeste com João Roma (PL). Ex-ministro da Cidadania de Jair Bolsonaro, que concorreu a uma vaga no Senado pela Bahia, e já tem uma relação consolidada com o partido de Flávio e seria o possível escolhido como uma grande liderança no campo da direita na Bahia.

Mapa mostra eleição votação para presidente nos dois turnos na Bahia — Foto: Arte g1

A situação de ACM Neto para os próximos anos já era de adversidade dupla mesmo antes do resultado do segundo turno, destaca Cláudio André. "Lula reeleito é catastrófico para ele. Talvez sobre, como estratégia de carreira política, repensar uma nova candidatura a prefeito de Salvador em 2028".

Com duas derrotas seguidas na disputa estadual, o cientista político Ariel Calmon aponta como um "desafio gigantesco" manter o futuro da oposição ao PT diante do resultado das eleições, mas um cenário diferente no próximo pleito nacional pode beneficiar Neto.

"Não dá para descartar que o grupo discuta outro nome para encabeçar a chapa, alguém com menos desgaste acumulado. Mas em 2030 não haverá Lula na urna, nem Jerônimo concorrendo à reeleição, o que abre espaço para oposição".

Para Cláudio, a base política de ACM Neto vai precisar ser testada nas urnas durante as eleições municipais, principalmente em cidades importantes, como Salvador, Feira de Santana, Vitória da Conquista, Camaçari e Lauro de Freitas.

"Pensando muito nessas maiores cidades, vai ser um grande teste de como a oposição vai chegar até lá e com indicativo de fortalecimento do campo governista. Se a gente pensar a montagem dessa chapa, como foi posta nessa eleição, a gente sabe que a força do PT está muito atrelada a uma aliança com o PSD, com o Avante e com o MDB. Devemos observar a partir de agora a montagem dos novos governos".

Por isso, Ariel Calmon ressalta como preocupação imediata segurar os prefeitos aliados, que costumam se aproximar do governo por depender de obras e recursos. A eleição municipal de 2028, principalmente em Salvador, mostrará se a oposição conseguiu se recompor.

"O caminho com mais chance de dar certo passa por construir uma centro-direita baiana com identidade própria, que fale de gestão e de problemas do estado sem depender de quem ocupa a polarização nacional. E isso exige tempo, novos nomes e presença contínua no interior", afirmou.

Um eventual apoio a Lula não representaria uma solução para ACM Neto na disputa pelo governo da Bahia no 1º turno e nem para o seu futuro político, avalia o cientista político Ariel Calmon.

"A trajetória de Neto e do grupo dele é de oposição ao PT, e uma adesão repentina seria lida como oportunismo. Além disso, a transferência de votos depende de quem empresta o prestígio. Quem orienta o voto lulista é o próprio Lula, e Lula estava no palanque de Jerônimo".

Ainda havia o risco do representante do União Brasil perder parte do eleitorado anti-PT nas cidades grandes, que sustenta a candidatura dele, diante das dificuldades de alcance no interior do estado. A disputa poderia, no máximo, ficar mais apertada e talvez fosse para um segundo turno, defende o cientista político.

"O lulista insatisfeito com Jerônimo existe, mas só seria conquistado com um trabalho de longo prazo, que apresentasse Neto como alternativa ao governo estadual sem confronto com o presidente".

Em 2022, quando Neto e Jerônimo se enfrentaram pela primeira vez na disputa pelo governo da Bahia, os dois chegaram ao segundo turno.

Neste ano, o representante do PT levou a melhor de primeira, com uma diferença expressiva. Jerônimo garantiu uma diferença superior a um milhão de votos em 2026.

No último pleito, o atual governador havia conseguido 700 mil votos a mais que Neto no primeiro turno e cerca de 480 mil no segundo.

ACM Neto em ato de campanha — Foto: Reprodução/TV Bahia

Os estudiosos também lembram que ACM Neto havia conquistado a liderança em cinco dos 27 territórios de identidade do estado em 2022. No pleito deste ano, ele manteve o domínio em apenas três.

🔎 Os territórios de identidade compreendem uma divisão de planejamento e gestão pública criada para organizar o estado. Diferentemente do modelo tradicional, que divide o espaço apenas por critérios puramente administrativos ou econômicos, eles agrupam municípios vizinhos que compartilham laços culturais, históricos, sociais, ambientais e econômicos semelhantes.

Cláudio André destacou a perda especialmente no sertão. Para ele, é uma disputa que deixou ACM Neto mais fraco. "Entendo que pesou a força do governismo, pesou também a questão da polarização nacional e eu entendo a atuação de vários prefeitos, mas há um ponto que a gente vai precisar investigar com mais exatidão. É talvez a construção de uma imagem mais popular do governador reeleito enquanto uma figura municipalista, enquanto um governador do interior".

A nacionalização da eleição e o primeiro turno estadual sem terceiros nomes forte, nem à direita e nem à esquerda, são dois pontos relevantes na disputa baiana no interior do estado, explica o cientista político Ariel Calmon. "Com Lula na urna e muito bem votado na Bahia, a disputa estadual virou uma espécie de plebiscito sobre estar com ele ou contra ele, e quem não está do lado de Lula perde terreno justamente nos municípios onde o lulismo é mais forte".

ACM Neto no Bahia Meio Dia — Foto: Reprodução/TV Bahia

Para os cientistas políticos, houve ainda um outro movimento errôneo de ACM Neto ao não se aproximar mais e por mais tempo do eleitor do interior.

"O erro de 2022 com o interior foi bem diagnosticado, tanto que a escolha do vice, a agenda de atos e as propostas regionais tentaram corrigir isso. Só que a aproximação veio durante a campanha e o eleitor do interior sabe distinguir quem aparece na eleição de quem está presente ao longo dos anos", destacou Ariel.

Junto com isso, conforme avaliou Calmon, a campanha ficou concentrada em Neto e em um núcleo pequeno do União Brasil, com pouco espaço para lideranças de outros partidos da base — o que afetou o tom e a presença nos territórios.

"Do outro lado havia uma fórmula já testada, com campanha alegre e propositiva, sem responder a ataques, mobilização orgânica de servidores, estudantes e movimentos, prefeituras espalhadas pelo estado e a foto com Lula em todo material", comparou.

Lula participou de convenção estadual do PT na Bahia, ao lado de Jerônimo Rodrigues — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert/ Presidência da República

Calmon classifica os eleitores do interior como aqueles que avaliam o governo de uma maneira de diferente, com um olhar retrospectivo. O eleitor olha para o que chegou à cidade dele, como estrada, cisterna, luz, saneamento e escola em tempo integral.

"Isso cria uma memória de gratidão com o grupo que governa o estado há 20 anos, e com Lula. Esse eleitor costuma ser mais conservador nos costumes, mas esse conservadorismo não se converte em voto na oposição, porque pesa mais a vontade de manter o que deu certo", pontuou.

Em municípios pequenos, que dependem de recursos do estado e da União, o apoio dos prefeitos a um candidato fazem a ponte entre o eleitor e o governo.

"Nas cidades maiores, o eleitor está mais exposto ao debate e à mídia, cobra mais os serviços urbanos, e o voto de oposição encontra mais espaço. Em Salvador e na região metropolitana, pesa ainda a passagem de Neto pela prefeitura, que deu a ele uma imagem própria de gestor, para além da figura de herdeiro do avô. Essa imagem não chegou ao interior, onde ele continua sendo visto como alguém da capital, associado ao carlismo".

Jerônimo Rodrigues celebra reeleição para o governo da Bahia — Foto: Rafael Cerqueira / g1 BA

Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT) foi reeleito governador da Bahia no dia 4 de outubro, no primeiro turno, com 55,80% dos votos, segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). Segundo colocado, ACM Neto (União Brasil) teve 43,72%. Os demais candidatos na disputa não chegaram a 1% dos votos individualmente: Ronaldo Mansur (PSOL) teve 0,33% dos votos; Aroldo Felix (UP), 0,06%; Maria Bona (PCO), 0,05%; e Ariel Capistrano (DC), 0,03%.

Ao todo, foram 8.291.090 votos válidos em todo o estado em 2026. Outros 233.096 (2,58%) votos foram em branco, e 521.993 (5,77%), nulos. A abstenção chegou a 2.258.135.

Procurada para comentar as estratégias pensadas para os próximos passos, a assessoria de ACM Neto não respondeu até a última atualização desta reportagem.

O político se pronunciou na condição de vice-presidente nacional do União Brasil, com um vídeo compartilhado nas redes sociais. Na mensagem, ACM Neto destacou o respeito pela democracia e pontuou a importância de se manter como oposição ao governo federal.

"Começando a planejar os próximos passos, deixando um recado muito claro: 'Quem ganhou deve governar, quem não ganhou deve fazer oposição'. E nós estamos preparados para fazer um trabalho, respeitando, é claro, a democracia, mas um trabalho com sinceridade, com verdade, mostrando os problemas da Bahia e do Brasil. Todos muito motivados, porque a gente tem a consciência que representa uma parcela importantíssima da população do nosso estado que não quer que essa esperança se apague", disse.

ACM publicou o vídeo um dia após Flávio Bolsonaro divulgar uma carta se declarando "presidente eleito" do Brasil. Pouco depois, o senador compartilhou uma nova versão do texto, trocando a expressão por "líder do Brasil.

Ele fugiu para os Estados Unidos, onde desembarcou na quarta-feira (28), após desobeder à ordem do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para que entregasse o passaporte à Polícia Federal (PF).

articles.title: Eleição de deputados: Câmara discute adoção do sistema distrital | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança na Constituição começou a avançar após eleições e ainda é negociada entre partidos políticos do centro, que buscam apoio do PT e de parte do PL.
articles.summary: Líderes da Câmara articulam a adoção do sistema distrital misto na eleição de deputados para frear a perda de espaço do centro após o crescimento expressivo do PL.
articles.body:
Líderes da Câmara dos Deputados e presidentes de partido articulam e pretendem retomar a tramitação de uma proposta que altera a forma de escolha dos deputados e institui o chamado sistema distrital misto. ( Entenda aqui como funciona )

O principal objetivo é frear a perda de espaço de partidos de centro no parlamento, após o crescimento do Partido Liberal ( PL ) nas eleições de 2026, que diminuiu o espaço de partidos do Centrão na Câmara e crescimento da ala bolsonarista.

A votação da proposta ainda está em negociação, mas a ideia é que as mudanças nas regras eleitorais comecem a valer integralmente nas eleições de 2034, com uma transição nas próximas eleições nacionais.

O PL terminou as eleições com 121 deputados, a maior bancada desde a Constituinte. Há quatro anos, o partido havia conseguido 99 deputados. Com o resultado deste ano, a sigla terá 23,6% das 513 cadeiras da Câmara dos Deputados.

Em contrapartida, o Centrão diminuiu sua presença. Perdeu 22 cadeiras em comparação com as eleições de 2022. Há entre os partidos do centro uma leitura de que mudanças precisam ser feitas para manter o poder dos partidos de centro.

Hugo Motta afirmou que pretende aprovar uma Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) instituindo o sistema distrital misto. A expectativa de líderes do centro é aprovar as mudanças ainda em 2026, ainda que admitam que as articulações estão somente no início.

Motta dialoga ainda com o presidente do Senado Federal, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), para agilizar a votação. Líderes esperam o apoio dos senadores porque as mudanças não afetam as eleições para eles. Mas o texto também ainda precisa de acordo na própria Câmara. Motta ainda tenta conseguir apoio do PT e do próprio PL.

O PL não tem interesse em mudar o sistema. Já entre os petistas, há resistência em alterar regras eleitorais logo depois de uma eleição acirrada. O medo é fornecer um aos apoiadores de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) um discurso de que há cerceamento ao partido bolsonarista.

Outros parlamentares dizem ainda que a mudança é tardia, que o perfil do Congresso já foi alterado.

O relator da PEC que ainda será apresentada deve ser o deputado Domingos Neto (PSD-CE), que já é o relator de um projeto de lei sobre o sistema distrital na Câmara.

Um dos pontos que ainda estão sendo negociados entre os líderes partidários qual modelo será adotado.

🔎 Atualmente, deputados são escolhidos de acordo com votos que eles e os seus partidos recebem. O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) realiza uma conta, chamada de quociente eleitoral, para definir quantos votos cada partido precisa para ter uma cadeira na Câmara dos Deputados. Esse modelo é chamado de sistema proporcional.

Essa fórmula acaba criando os chamados "puxadores de votos" — um candidato que recebe muitos votos e ,indiretamente, contribue para a eleição de candidatos que não obtiveram o número suficiente de votos.

No sistema distrital, cada estado brasileiro é dividido em distritos. Cada distrito elege um número específico de deputados. Os moradores dessa determinada região poderão votar apenas nos candidatos do distrito em que vivem. São eleitos os candidatos os mais votados no distrito.

Mas, buscando manter uma parte do poder dos partidos no processo eleitoral, os deputados estudam criar um modelo misto:

metade das vagas do distrito ficariam com os mais votados;

a outra metade distribuída seguindo uma lista de candidatos definida previamente pelos partidos. As vagas seriam dividas de acordo com a quantidade de votos que as siglas conseguirem. Por exemplo: se um partido obtem votos para eleger quatro deputados, são eleitos os quatro primeiros nomes da lista.

O distrital misto tem como defensores presidentes de partidos como Gilberto Kassab, do PSD, e Ciro Nogueira, do Progressistas. Mas não há consenso no Congresso Nacional.

Apesar de defender o modelo, a deputada Adriana Ventura (Novo-SP), aponta algumas preocupações, como o sistema deixar a disputa mais vulnerável ao crime organizado, com candidatos de facções ou milícias controlando alguns distritos.

Parlamentares do PSOL também são críticos ao distrital misto por entenderem que o modelo prejudicaria o partido. Apontam, ainda, o risco de reduzir a participação de grupos que já são minoria no Congresso, como mulheres e negros.

Muitos deputados defendem um quarto modelo, o chamado distritão: transformar a eleição da Câmara em majoritária. Ou seja, os deputados mais votados em cada estado são eleitos, sem os chamados "puxadores de votos".

O modelo é criticado por especialistas, que dizem que ele pode facilitar a eleição de candidatos com mais recursos e dificultar a renovação no Congresso Nacioanl. A Câmara tentou aprovar a mudança para este modelo em 2017 e 2021, mas não houve votos suficientes para aprovar a mudança.

Deputado mais votado no Rio de Janeiro, o líder do PP, deputado Luizinho, é a favor do modelo e diz que, para não enfraquecer os partidos, a proposta poderia prever que o mandato pertence às legendas, diferentemente de outras eleições majoritárias, e o deputado não poderia trocar de filiação.

Plenário da Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: Bruno Spada / Câmara dos Deputados

Para angariar apoio, os líderes indicaram que as mudanças não valeriam para as próximas eleições, em 2030. Nela, haveria uma transição. Mas os detalhes de como isso seria feito não foram definidos, segundo o relator Domingos Neto.

Parlamentares ouvidos pelo g1 e pela GloboNews, dizem que existe a ideia de fazer um distritão em 2030 para atender os deputados que defendem esse modelo. Depois, em 2034, entraria em vigor o distrital misto, com a lista fechada dos partidos.

Domingos Neto afirma que a lista dos partidos deverá seguir as regras de inclusão e cotas de mulheres e negros e pardos para candidaturas. Mas ainda há dúvidas sobre como a diversidade de eleitos seria garantida se os partidos puderem definir a ordem da lista.

Em 2034, os eleitores votariam assim, somente uma vez, para deputado em cada distrito, para eleger deputados, e esses votos seriam contabilizados no estado para a definição de forma proporcional de quantas vagas cada sigla poderia preencher a partir da lista dos partidos.

Um dos pontos que levam a mais dúvidas entre os deputados é a divisão dos estados em distritos. Deputados estão preocupados com os votos que hoje são espalhados em várias cidades que podem pertencer a distritos diferentes.

Domingos Neto afirma que a definição dos distritos seria feita a partir de critérios do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) e uma comissão mista do Congresso acompanharia a implementação.

Por outro lado, defensores indicam que o processo eleitoral ficaria mais barato, já que o candidato não precisaria fazer campanha em todo o estado, somente em seu distrito.

Também dizem que o distrital misto aproximaria o candidato dos problemas reais dos eleitores, ao se concentrarem em uma região menor.

articles.title: Dia de Todos os Santos: conheça lugar com santos gigantes em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: A data em celebração ocorre um dia antes do Dia dos Finados, em 2 de novembro. Às margens da SP-425, na região de Presidente Prudente (SP), espaço dedicado reúne quase 20 imagens de santos católicos.
articles.summary: Neste domingo (1º), quando a Igreja Católica celebra o Dia de Todos os Santos, um espaço às SP-425 reúne representações religiosas gigantes, em um convite à fé e à devoção.
articles.body:
Neste domingo (1º), quando a Igreja Católica celebra o Dia de Todos os Santos, um espaço criado no interior de São Paulo r eúne representações religiosas gigantes, em um convite à fé e à devoção às vésperas do Dia de Finados (2).

As imagens de diferentes santos com até 10 metros de altura estão localizadas às margens da Rodovia Assis Chateaubriand (SP-425), entre Presidente Prudente e Regente Feijó .

Até a última atualização, o espaço reunia quase 20 representações religiosas e foi criado em 2020 . Segundo o empresário Agesner Monteiro, havia previsão de acrescentar novas imagens, como o Sagrado Coração de Jesus, Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe e São José.

“O Caminho dos Devotos continua sendo pensado e construído de forma gradual, sempre com o objetivo de levar fé, acolhimento e devoção às pessoas que visitam o espaço”, disse ao g1 .

O significado do local é ainda mais simbólico e espiritual, já que o morador teve a ideia após a experiência de viver um milagre com o filho, que motivou a construção do espaço como forma de expressar fé, agradecimento e devoção.

Caminho dos Devotos, entre Presidente Prudente e Regente Feijó, no interior paulista — Foto: Beatriz Jarins/g1

A Conferência Nacional dos Bispos do Brasil (CNBB) publicou uma solenidade feita pelo Cardeal Orani João Tempesta, arcebispo do Rio de Janeiro (RJ), que traz mais detalhes sobre o Dia de Todos os Santos.

Segundo o cardeal, o fato de a celebração ocorrer antes do Dia dos Finados, que homenageia os entes que já morreram, é justamente porque, a partir do olhar católico, “a meta de todo cristão é a vida eterna.”

“Num dia rezamos por todos os santos que contemplam a face de Deus e, no outro dia, rezamos por nossos entes queridos já falecidos, almejando um dia encontrarmos com eles. Na Solenidade de Todos os Santos, rezamos pedindo a graça da santificação, e no Dia de Finados, rezamos a Deus pela graça de alcançar a vida eterna”, disse o cardeal, segundo a CNBB.

Isso porque a Igreja Católica acredita na intercessão de Todos os Santos por cada pessoa. “Eles não operam o milagre, mas intercedem por nós junto a Deus. E, ao contrário do que algumas pessoas dizem, sobretudo de outras religiões, nós não adoramos imagem, mas veneramos, respeitamos, e o milagre vem de Deus; eles intercedem por nós”, reforçou o cardeal.

Ao g1 , o padre Armando Nochetti, de Presidente Prudente, explicou que o Dia de Todos os Santos celebra todas as pessoas que já alcançaram o paraíso e estão na presença de Deus. Já o Dia de Finados, segundo o padre, é dedicado à memória e à oração por todos os fiéis que já morreram.

"Especialmente aqueles que ainda passam por um processo de purificação no purgatório, antes de chegarem à plenitude da santidade", descreve.

Segundo o padre Armando, a Igreja faz na liturgia uma homenagem a todos os santos e mártires, sejam eles conhecidos oficialmente pela Igreja ou anônimos que já alcançaram a vida eterna no céu. "Todos nós, por meio do batismo, somos chamados a viver a santidade, seguindo os exemplos de Cristo, que nos deixou em seus quatro evangelhos o caminho da santidade."

"No Dia de Todos os Santos, os fiéis católicos devem participar da Santa Missa, já que a data é uma solenidade e um dia de preceito (obrigação), a fim de que possamos refletir sobre o chamado à santidade e fazer um propósito de vivê-la em nosso dia a dia."

Já no Caminho dos Devotos, o responsável, Agesner Monteiro, afirmou que, na data, especificamente, não estava prevista celebração especial. No entanto, ele, junto com a Igreja, estava organizando uma missa regular na capela, que deve ocorrer no primeiro domingo de cada mês.

“Criando um momento permanente de oração e encontro para os visitantes e devotos”, afirma Agesner.

Segundo o responsável, a visitação no santuário às margens da rodovia cresce gradativamente, sem uma estimativa para outubro, mas, até abril deste ano, a estimativa era de aproximadamente 10 mil pessoas visitando o local mensalmente.

Além disso, o local já recebeu turistas que viajaram quase 10 mil quilômetros para conhecer o espaço , com previsão de novas imagens no local. Confira abaixo a lista de esculturas instaladas no local até outubro:

“O Caminho dos Devotos continua sendo pensado e construído de forma gradual, sempre com o objetivo de levar fé, acolhimento e devoção às pessoas que visitam o espaço”, completa.
