articles.body:
An advisor to Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) said Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) cannot disinvite his former primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) from a scheduled event on Sunday in Detroit, Mich.

“This is not Abdul’s event,” Antjuan Seawright, an advisor to Clyburn, told The New York Times Saturday afternoon. “The invitation still stands.”

El-Sayed was originally scheduled to appear at a church in Detroit alongside Stevens and Clyburn, but he asked his former primary opponent to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from Sunday’s event.

The relationship between El-Sayed and Stevens has grown tense in the past few days. The tension stemmed from a political ad supporting El-Sayed’s campaign that appeared to blame Israel and Jews for rising costs of living.

Stevens released a statement saying the Democratic Senate nominee did not condemn the ad forcefully enough.

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

El-Sayed fired back in a statement posted to the social platform X, saying, “so while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics.”

Recently, Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish said he would not support El-Sayed in the upcoming elections and accused the Democrat of using antisemitic language on the campaign trail. But Stevens reaffirmed that she would continue to back the Democratic Senate candidate.

Israel has been the center of attention in the days leading up to the midterm elections where El-Sayed has maintained a critical stance throughout.

The Senate race between El-Sayed and his GOP opponent Mike Rogers has been intense with a recent CNN poll showing 49 percent of respondents leaning toward the Democrat and 42 percent toward the Republican. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ leans heavily in favor of El-Sayed, giving him a 74 percent chance of winning.

articles.title: Alaska officials ask judge to deny Trump administration’s ‘impossible’ demand to set aside Senate ballots
articles.summary: The Republican-led state government in Alaska implored a federal judge on Saturday to permanently dismiss the Trump administration’s lawsuit that seeks to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race if GOP Sen.
articles.body: The Republican-led state government in Alaska implored a federal judge on Saturday to permanently dismiss the Trump administration’s lawsuit that seeks to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race if GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses. “The United States’ opposition provides no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer,” the filing said, adding that “the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters’ vital right to ballot secrecy.” The filing from Alaska officials comes just three days before Election Day and as the judge is expected to rule soon on whether to dismiss the lawsuit or continue with it. The Trump administration has claimed that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting a retired teacher with the same name as Sullivan to run in the race, creating confusion that it says will unfairly take away votes intended for the incumbent. Peltola has denied the allegations. The Trump administration filed a lawsuit Oct. 22 against local election officials, arguing that the results of the competitive Senate race should not be certified unless Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is declared the winner. Alaska officials on Saturday criticized the legal basis on which the Trump administration has argued it has standing to intervene in the election, as election certification is left up to the states. The filing noted that the Alaska Supreme Court approved the second Sullivan’s name to be on the ballot months ago and added that “state officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion.” Alaska officials also took aim at the Justice Department’s proposal of “segregating” ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan, writing, “this unexplained idea makes no sense.” “No matter how the ballots are physically stored, it will be easy to tell which ballots rank Daniel J.,” the filing said. “If the United States means something different — as it seems to — its ballot segregation proposal is both disturbing and impossible.” The Alaska attorney general’s office asked the judge to “immediately dismiss this lawsuit with prejudice and allow state officials to conduct the general election — including ballot counting and certification — free from unwarranted federal interference.” The Trump administration amended its complaint this week to cite new reporting from The New York Times, which alleged that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan and that Peltola herself was aware of the situation. The Times story citied a former campaign manager who later attempted to retract her statements. At a rally Friday night, Peltola told a crowd of her supporters that she was “so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s candidacy.” “I want fewer candidates in the primary. I’m not out soliciting more competition,” Peltola said, adding she did “not need any help” defeating Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan took aim at Peltola in a Fox News interview on Saturday, saying that “there’s no way Peltola doesn’t know about” the scheme to recruit Dan J. Sullivan. “It’s deception. But at its worst, it’s disdain for us Alaskans,” he said. “Think about what they did. They’re trying to make sure that Alaskans throw away their vote.”

articles.body:
The Republican-led state government in Alaska implored a federal judge on Saturday to permanently dismiss the Trump administration's lawsuit that seeks to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race if GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses.

"The United States' opposition provides no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer," the filing said, adding that "the relief demanded is inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters' vital right to ballot secrecy."

The filing from Alaska officials comes just three days before Election Day and as the judge is expected to rule soon on whether to dismiss the lawsuit or continue with it.

The Trump administration has claimed that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting a retired teacher with the same name as Sullivan to run in the race, creating confusion that it says will unfairly take away votes intended for the incumbent. Peltola has denied the allegations.

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit Oct. 22 against local election officials, arguing that the results of the competitive Senate race should not be certified unless Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is declared the winner.

Alaska officials on Saturday criticized the legal basis on which the Trump administration has argued it has standing to intervene in the election, as election certification is left up to the states.

The filing noted that the Alaska Supreme Court approved the second Sullivan's name to be on the ballot months ago and added that "state officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion."

Alaska officials also took aim at the Justice Department's proposal of "segregating" ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan, writing, "this unexplained idea makes no sense."

"No matter how the ballots are physically stored, it will be easy to tell which ballots rank Daniel J.," the filing said. "If the United States means something different — as it seems to — its ballot segregation proposal is both disturbing and impossible."

The Alaska attorney general's office asked the judge to "immediately dismiss this lawsuit with prejudice and allow state officials to conduct the general election — including ballot counting and certification — free from unwarranted federal interference."

The Trump administration amended its complaint this week to cite new reporting from The New York Times , which alleged that Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan and that Peltola herself was aware of the situation. The Times story citied a former campaign manager who later attempted to retract her statements.

At a rally Friday night, Peltola told a crowd of her supporters that she was "so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else's candidacy."

"I want fewer candidates in the primary. I'm not out soliciting more competition," Peltola said, adding she did "not need any help" defeating Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan took aim at Peltola in a Fox News interview on Saturday, saying that "there's no way Peltola doesn't know about" the scheme to recruit Dan J. Sullivan.

"It's deception. But at its worst, it's disdain for us Alaskans," he said. "Think about what they did. They're trying to make sure that Alaskans throw away their vote."

articles.title: Trump calls $50 million contract for ex-lawyer Habba Mildon 'not acceptable'
articles.summary: PALM BEACH, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Saturday it was "unacceptable" for one of his ‌former lawyers, Alina Habba Mildon, to secure a...
articles.body:
PALM BEACH, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Saturday it was "unacceptable" for one of his ‌former lawyers, Alina Habba Mildon, to secure a $50 million contract for ‌herself while working at the US Department of Justice.

"I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, ​and it's not acceptable," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. "Not acceptable at all."

The New York Times reported last week that the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a Venezuelan banker facing US felony bribery charges before ‌striking a plea deal in ⁠August 2025, guaranteed Habba Mildon more than $50 million over four years. The deal, according to the newspaper, would pay $10 million a ⁠year plus bonuses.

Trump said he told Habba Mildon he did not want her to be paid and called the episode "terrible."

Habba Mildon was serving as the acting US attorney ​in New ​Jersey when she signed the contract with ​Herrera's family company, Concord Partners, ‌days after it was registered in late October 2025, the New York Times reported.

By the time she started her employment with the Herrera family, a court had disqualified her from serving as US attorney. She resigned on December 8 and was appointed a senior adviser to the attorney general the same day, ‌and was still in that role when, ​according to the New York Times, she started ​at Concord on January 1.

Trump ​pardoned Herrera on January 15, 2026, according to the Justice ‌Department's website.

Habba Mildon last week said ​she was never paid ​for a pardon, never met with anyone at the White House or Justice Department about a pardon, and never did any work for ​a pardon for anyone.

The ‌Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(Reporting by ​Gram Slattery in Palm Beach and Jasper Ward in Washington; ​Editing by Sergio Non and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
articles.summary: The state's $500m Senate race may be the most closely watched in the US midterms, and is about far more than control of Congress.
articles.body:
The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.

For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.

But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.

That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.

"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.

These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.

For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.

At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.

In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual.

"It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."

When Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters – with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.

He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate.

"Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."

The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning – "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" – is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.

His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music. He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.

In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state.

"A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."

For Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.

At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump – alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton – was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size.

"If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.

Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans.

"Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."

Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X.

"When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."

For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.

They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.

"I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser.

"The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."

For the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics – a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser.

"Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."

But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.

The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one.

Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.

Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.

Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.

Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters – many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 – have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies.

Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.

Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state – a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability.

"It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."

Then there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.

The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement.

"Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."

The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud – later dropped – and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges.

The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.

All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics – and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.

Talarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.

Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas.

Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race . Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.

While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state – spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.

They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries – two powerful interests in the state.

Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".

Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.

The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.

He frequently leans into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.

There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late – the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath.

"We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."

But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.

Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.

Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.

Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again.

"I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

articles.title: US midterms: 2 days to go – Who leads in the polls as Trump rallies
articles.summary: Democrats remain ahead in national polls as Trump and candidates make their final push in the days before polling day.
articles.body:
With two days to the United States midterm elections , Democratic and Republican leaders are making last-ditch efforts to woo voters, with the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points.

According to the latest survey, Democrats are still ahead of the Republicans, but several closely fought Senate races may decide which party ends up in control of the US Congress .

On Sunday, President Donald Trump will be campaigning in Iowa and Kansas , while Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate who has faced an increased wave of Islamophobic attacks, will be holding events in Michigan.

What do the latest US midterm polls say?

Democrats continue to lead Republicans by 51.5 percent to 43.1 percent, according to the latest RealClearPolling average.

A national THP/MM survey conducted on October 28 and 29 put Democrats ahead by 54 percent to 41 percent, while an Emerson College poll conducted from October 24 to 26 showed a 10-point Democratic lead.

Natalie Jackson, a political analyst and pollster, told Al Jazeera that the results reflected public dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy .

“Polling shows an environment that is pretty favourable to the Democrats. The president is very unpopular, Americans feel the pinch of high costs, which are partly due to tariffs and the war in Iran, and the general sentiment is that Republicans did not deliver in the last two years.”

In Kansas, a Washington Post-Schar School poll released on Friday suggested Democrat Adam Hamilton was leading against Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 52 percent to 43 percent.

But another Emerson College survey indicated a tighter race, with Hamilton ahead of Marshall by 50 percent to 47percent.

Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former communications director for the Republican National Committee, questioned the nine-point lead of the Washington Post-Schar School survey.

“I don’t know how it plays out, but, you know, we saw an outlier poll in Iowa just two years ago that caused a lot of damage to the whole polling industry,” Heye said.

He was referring to a Des Moines Register poll published days before the 2024 presidential election that showed Kamala Harris leading Trump by three percentage points in Iowa. Trump went on to win the state by about 13 points, a difference of 16 points from the poll’s margin.

“A lot of Republicans just don’t want to answer calls from pollsters,” he added.

Jackson, the political analyst, also said polling might not accurately reflect the result of individual Senate contests.

“In some individual races – particularly the close Senate races – we could see polling error that shifts the race in one direction or another,” she said.

“Pollsters have reported some potential issues with getting Republicans to answer polls. That might indicate that polls are underestimating Republicans, but we don’t know until the votes are counted.”

What happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

As the election nears, both parties are focusing their final campaign messages on the economy and the cost of living .

While Democrats have been focusing on affordability issues, Trump has been conducting telephone rallies for Republican candidates in closely contested races.

Heye said Republicans were struggling to convince voters that their economic policies would improve the situation in the country.

Asked whether Republicans had found a convincing closing message, he said: “No, they haven’t. That’s a big part of their challenge.”

The Republican strategist said candidates should focus on issues voters were raising, particularly the cost of energy, healthcare, groceries and other everyday expenses.

“Families are making very real economic decisions; you have to address to them what you’re going to do to solve those problems,” Heye said.

Celinda Lake, a Democratic strategist and pollster working with El-Sayed’s campaign in Michigan, said Democrats were also facing questions about what they would deliver if they controlled Congress.

“The feelings about the Democrats are negative, too, which is very different from, say, 2018, when Democrats were positively perceived,” she said.

Lake said while many voters were seeking change, they were still unsure what either of the parties would do.

Where will Trump, El-Sayed and other candidates campaign today?

Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. The president had initially cancelled both appearances before reversing his decision on Friday.

In Iowa, in one of the contested Senate races, Trump will campaign with Republican US Representative Ashley, who faces Democrat Josh Turek. In Kansas, Senator Marshall is also looking for re-election against Democrat Adam Hamilton in a tight contest.

This state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but rising farming costs and opposition to Trump’s immigration crackdown have made this race unexpectedly competitive.

Heye said Trump should not have cancelled the appearances in the first place.

“They never should have been cancelled to begin with,” he said. “Whether they help or not, they certainly help Trump to show that I’m out there trying to do the things to get my people over the line.”

Meanwhile, El-Sayed is scheduled to campaign in Detroit and Southfield, Michigan, as he seeks to defeat Republican Mike Rogers in the Senate race.

Lake, who is working with El-Sayed’s campaign, said the candidate had made affordability key to his message.

“He’s very clear. He says, ‘Money out of politics, money in your pockets, and healthcare for all.'”

She said the Michigan race would depend heavily on voter turnout.

“I think the race is going to be really close. What we’re looking at is turnout,” she said.

More than 51 million Americans have already voted, according to reports. Both parties have encouraged voters to cast their ballots using the mail-in system or make plans to vote on Tuesday.

But early-voting numbers do not show which party will win, because they do not establish how those voters voted.

Lake, the Democratic strategist, said turnout would be one of the most important factors in the elections.

“Did Trump really rally the Republicans? Did the Democrats come out in record numbers?” she asked.

She also identified young voters and the gender gap as important indicators to follow during the election.

Jackson, the political analyst, said the final two days will probably not bring major changes to the national political environment.

“It’s unlikely that anything really shifts in the national environment. We could see some local developments in some of these races, but by now things are pretty locked in.”

A total of 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are up for grabs.

Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to win the majority in both chambers.

While polling suggests Democrats are ahead, control of the Senate will depend on individual contests, including races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Alaska.

Jackson said the polling provided a clearer picture of the national political environment than the likely outcome of individual Senate races.

“We can be fairly confident that Democrats will win the House majority, but the Senate picture is unclear,” she told Al Jazeera.

Heye, the Republican strategist, also pointed to the differences between the House and Senate contests.

“The Senate is so campaign-, state- and candidate-specific. It’s a much harder read,” he said.

Candidates have Sunday and Monday to make their final appeals to voters before they head to the polls on Tuesday.

Polling stations will begin closing on Tuesday evening, with the first results expected shortly afterwards. However, some of the closely fought races might take longer.

Heye said he would be watching the first results in Indiana and Kentucky for indications of how the election might unfold.

“Yeah, I start with the two states that close earliest, which are Indiana and Kentucky,” he said.

But Jackson cautioned that the results in individual Senate races could differ from what the final polls suggest.

“That is always possible with polling,” she said, adding that the scale and direction of any polling errors would become clear once the votes were counted.

articles.title: 'Toxic cocktail' of renter protections destroyed $39M affordable housing investment as Dem cities follow suit
articles.summary: A once-profitable apartment complex saw rent collections plunge as Seattle expanded restrictions on landlords, sparking a constitutional battle with national implications.
articles.body: Seattle's effort to protect renters allegedly helped destroy a $39 million investment meant to provide affordable housing, sending a 254-unit apartment complex that served lower-income residents into receivership. Now, its owners have scored a court victory in a battle that could influence similar fights in Philadelphia and other Democrat-led cities. The Washington Court of Appeals ruled Monday that GRE Downtowner LLC, the company behind Seattle's 254-unit Addison on Fourth affordable housing development, can proceed with claims that the city's sweeping rental regulations amounted to an unconstitutional taking of private property. GRE alleges the restrictions, including an ordinance requiring landlords to accommodate certain additional occupants without their consent, sent rent collections plummeting, triggered millions in losses and ultimately made the once-viable affordable housing investment financially unsustainable. The development operated under the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, which offers tax incentives to private investors in exchange for providing rent-restricted apartments to lower-income residents. Sean Flynn, executive director of the Rental Housing Association of Washington, explained that while such developments typically generate relatively modest profits, the federal tax credits make them financially attractive to investors, helping bring private money into affordable housing projects that might otherwise struggle to get built. Flynn, who is working with GRE Downtowner in its case against the City of Seattle, told Fox News Digital that the city's successive ordinances targeting landlords ultimately created a "toxic cocktail of legislation" that took a functioning affordable housing property and "destroyed it." PROPERTY OWNER ADVOCACY GROUPS PUSH BACK ON MAMDANI'S 'RENTAL RIPOFF REPORT,' PUBLIC DATABASE OF LANDLORDS According to court filings, GRE's investment initially proved financially viable, with the property generating positive cash flow from 2015 through 2018. But as Seattle enacted a series of ordinances restricting criminal-background checks, expanding tenants' ability to bring additional occupants into their apartments, limiting certain evictions and requiring relocation assistance following qualifying rent increases, GRE alleges its rent collections collapsed from 93.9% in 2018 to just 44.1% in 2023, contributing to nearly $5.8 million in cumulative operating losses. The financial deterioration ultimately culminated in a federal judge appointing a receiver in January 2026 to take control of the property following a mortgage default. "The policies they're passing are detrimental to the folks they're actually trying to help," Flynn warned, arguing that excessive restrictions on landlords ultimately hurt renters by discouraging housing investment. "No one will invest to build more housing if they believe that the government can come in and effectuate a taking – to take the property out from under them – and they have no legal recourse." OREGON DEMOCRATS PROPOSE 'RIGHT TO REST ACT' DECRIMINALIZING PUBLIC CAMPING AS HOMELESS CRISIS SURGES "What this decision says is government, you can regulate, you can regulate to your heart's content," Flynn added. "But if your regulations amount to the point of which you take my real property, I'm allowed to sue you for it." Ilya Somin, a George Mason University law professor specializing in constitutional law and property rights, told Fox News Digital that the ruling is more consequential than a routine procedural decision but cautioned against overstating its broader impact. "This is only moderately significant, but it's more significant than just a routine legal decision that only affects the people immediately involved," Somin said, explaining that courts in other states could consider the Washington ruling when weighing similar constitutional challenges. He also said the case could theoretically go to the U.S. Supreme Court, but said that was fairly unlikely. Seattle is hardly alone in imposing sweeping restrictions on landlords. San Francisco has long enforced rent controls and limits on evictions, and New York City expanded eviction protections in 2024 under the state's Good Cause Eviction law, limiting landlords' ability to remove certain tenants or refuse lease renewals while allowing renters to challenge excessive rent increases. Portland, Oregon, limits landlords' use of criminal histories when screening prospective tenants and requires relocation payments following certain rent increases of 10% or more. Philadelphia has also adopted restrictions involving criminal-history screening. These policies reflect a broader push to strengthen renters' rights in major Democrat-led cities, even as property owners raise concerns about the consequences of increasingly restrictive housing regulations. OBAMA-ERA MANDATE SLASHED AFTER BEING BLAMED FOR 'SKYROCKETING' HOUSING COSTS Flynn warned that the consequences of Seattle's housing policies extend well beyond Addison on Fourth, arguing that mounting restrictions have driven developers and smaller landlords away from Seattle — a city once bustling with residential construction. "Once upon a time in Seattle, you could stand from my office and you could see crane after crane after crane building housing," Flynn said. "They're gone, and they're not coming back." Flynn argued that the resulting decline in investment ultimately hurts ordinary renters, leaving them with fewer housing options and higher costs. "When you take the investment incentive out of providing a product, you get worse products at a higher cost," he said. "Investors listen and they vote with their feet. And as a result, there's less housing and the housing that is available is of lesser quality." NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN' GRE's lawsuit seeks compensation under a legal principle known as inverse condemnation, which allows property owners to pursue payment when they believe government actions have effectively taken or damaged their property without providing just compensation. GRE argues that Seattle's ordinances, individually and collectively, went so far in restricting its property rights that the city should be held financially responsible for the resulting losses. The Seattle City Attorney's Office told Fox News Digital that officials are reviewing the appellate ruling and weighing their next steps. "We haven't made a decision on an appeal yet," Chief of Staff Dan Nolte said in an email Thursday. "I believe the plaintiffs in this case deserve to win at least on that roommate provision," Somin told Fox News Digital, referring to Seattle's restrictions on landlords' ability to exclude certain additional occupants from rental properties. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Somin pointed to the Supreme Court's 6-3 decision in Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid , which ruled that a California regulation requiring agricultural employers to allow union organizers onto their private property constituted a physical taking under the Fifth Amendment. He argued that Seattle's Roommate Ordinance raises a similar constitutional question because it requires landlords to accommodate additional occupants with whom they never entered into a rental agreement. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I think the strongest per se argument is simply an argument against this provision of the ordinance, which says they have to take these people who they never made any contract with at all, never screened, and so on," Somin said. "The additional requirement to let them on their land is going beyond what's in the contract, and the same thing you know would apply here in the Seattle case."

articles.title: Pablo Iglesias desvía el foco y señala la liberalización de la Alta Velocidad como problema: "Este sí es el debate político"
articles.standfirst: Para el exlider de Podemos el dilema está entre la privatización y la seguridad de los usuarios
articles.summary: Para el exlider de Podemos el dilema está entre la privatización y la seguridad de los usuarios
articles.body: Las recientes declaraciones de Pablo Iglesias en Malas Lenguas de RTVE han vuelto a poner sobre la mesa el debate en torno al modelo ferroviario español y su seguridad. El expolítico expresó su "perplejidad" ante la gravedad de que, en un margen de nueve meses, se hayan producido dos de los siniestros más graves de la historia ferroviaria nacional, un hecho que considera "inasumible para España". Para Iglesias, la clave de esta problemática radica en un dato temporal evidente: ambos accidentes se han registrado después del proceso de liberalización del sector de la alta velocidad. Durante su intervención, el exdirigente arrancó recordando "una cosa que dijo Pedro Sánchez, yo creo que con perplejidad, que es verdad, dijo: Es inasumible para España que en nueve meses se produzcan dos de los accidentes más graves de toda la historia ferroviaria de nuestro país en el marco de nueve meses". En su análisis, Iglesias contrapone el histórico del servicio con la situación actual: "Claro, ahí hay un dato. El dato es que la alta velocidad en España existe desde el 92' y que los dos accidentes más graves se han producido después del proceso de liberalización del sistema de la alta velocidad en España". Además, enfatizó el papel de las representaciones de los trabajadores en este conflicto: "Esto es lo que dicen los sindicatos. Los sindicatos dicen: Desde el momento en el que ustedes liberalizaron, dejaron que entraran nuevas empresas; desde el momento en el que se empezaron a usar subcontratas para asumir tareas de seguridad, nosotros trabajamos peor, y hay peor seguridad para nosotros y peor seguridad para los usuarios, y por eso los maquinistas convocaban una huelga antes de que se produjera el accidente». Cuestionando las peticiones de dimisión en el ministerio de Transportes, señaló: "Este sí es el debate político. A mí me ha enfadado escuchar en ciertas voces de la izquierda: Que dimita el ministro. No, que dimita el ministro no. Vamos a discutir si el proceso de liberalización de la Alta Velocidad en España es lo que puede estar detrás de que ahora los trenes sean más menos seguros que antes. Y entonces hay muchos que tienen que asumir la responsabilidad de haber votado a favor: el PP, el PSOE y Ciudadanos. Los partidos de la izquierda votaron en contra de la liberalización". Tras ser preguntado sobre la normativa comunitaria, respondió: "Muy buena pregunta. Pues en Francia, la manera que tuvieron de aplicar la directiva europea fue mantener en Francia y en Alemania el 90 % del control en manos públicas y cobrar un canon el doble de caro a las privadas que lo que se cobra en España. En España fuimos campeones de abaratar el mercado y permitir a los italianos y a los franceses que entraran pagando menos que en cualquier otro país. De hecho, estas dos compañías, después del accidente de Adamuz, dijeron que les rebajaran 119 millones porque no estaban pagando bien". Una intervención en el programa en la cadena pública que concluyó señalando el fondo estructural de la cuestión: "A lo mejor, como están diciendo los sindicatos, el problema político no es un ministro, el problema político fue tomar la decisión de liberalizar un sistema que estaba funcionando mejor y con más seguridad cuando era puramente público".

articles.title: Midterm voters reveal what's driving them to the polls — but what they're voting against may matter more
articles.summary: Voters reveal frustration with Trump's administration and opposition to socialism as the key factors driving their midterm election decisions.
articles.body: With just two days until Americans head to the polls, voters from across the country revealed that their midterm decisions may be driven more by frustration with what they oppose than by support for what they believe in. "The Democrats down the line because Trump is an idiot," one voter from Colorado said when asked by Fox News Digital how he plans to vote. "I'm a Democratic voter," Lucy from Washington, D.C., said. "I am sick of the administration. I have been very upset about what's happening to this city and this area and this country — all the lies." TRUMP'S NOT ON THE BALLOT BUT SWING STATE VOTERS STILL CAST BALLOTS WITH MAGA IN MIND Despite President Donald Trump not appearing on the midterm ballot, most Democrat voters whom Fox News Digital spoke with cited his administration as their driving factor to vote for Democrats for this year’s congressional slate. "Democrats," Mark from Utah said about who he is voting for. "Because of corruption, cost of living, democracy. It doesn't seem like this administration cares about the Constitution. The president's enriching himself and the rest of the country is getting more poor." Control of Congress is at stake in the midterms, with Democrats seeking to gain enough seats to challenge Trump's legislative agenda during the remainder of his presidency. One Democrat voter even acknowledged his agreement with some Republican policies, but noted his opposition to Trump outweighs his right-leaning stances. "I generally vote Democrat," Jeremy from New York said. He continued, "It's funny because I agree with a lot of the Republican stances. I just feel like when you get behind someone who's unfortunately in charge, like the man that is, then this is something I can't really support." FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS IRAN LOOMS LARGE, CAN THE GOP KEEP THE FAITHFUL? Another voter said he voted for Trump and Republicans in previous elections, but has decided to vote Democrat in the upcoming election because he claims there was a lack of follow-through by the Trump administration. "After six years of Make America Great Again, we're not great again," one voter from Virginia said. "So I'm switching." Opposition wasn't limited to Democrat voters. The few voters who told Fox News Digital they planned to vote Republican also expressed concerns about the opposing party as major factors in their midterm decisions. "I'm voting Republican," Yago said. "The reason why is because I do not want to see socialism in this country. Socialism did nothing but destroy everything." "First off, just social policies," John from Illinois said about what’s motivating him to vote red. "I think that over the past couple of years, we've seen what the Democrats promote, as far as social policies go, and family policy, gender policy, all that stuff. I think particularly abortion, too." Other voters pointed to specific issues driving their decisions, including immigration enforcement, foreign policy, gun rights and the economy. "My main concern is probably just everything that's happening with ICE and DHS," Emily from Texas, who plans to vote Democrat, said. FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE Another voter who pledged to support Republicans said his decision "comes down to gun control." "The Second Amendment protects your First [Amendment]," Nelson from Washington, D.C., said. "When it comes to foreign policy with helping out Israel and not giving any help to Palestine," Kamil from Washington said, "That's what's driving me to vote for the Democrats instead." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For some Americans, the midterm elections are shaping up to be less about enthusiasm for either political party and more about opposition to the direction they believe the country is heading.

articles.title: GOP plan for lame-duck sprint runs into votes, rules and the calendar
articles.summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are poised to clash in the lame duck over how far to push President Trump’s agenda. Midterm voters are widely expected to give Democrats control of the House, and maybe the Senate, in the next Congress, which would bring Trump’s legislative agenda to a screeching halt beginning next year. That scenario…
articles.body:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are poised to clash in the lame duck over how far to push President Trump’s agenda.

Midterm voters are widely expected to give Democrats control of the House, and maybe the Senate, in the next Congress, which would bring Trump’s legislative agenda to a screeching halt beginning next year.

That scenario is setting off alarm bells among one camp of Republicans pushing to extend the post-election session to maximize the passage of GOP policies while they still have the power to do so. That includes a so-called reconciliation package designed to move partisan priorities without the need for any Democratic support.

“Republicans should unequivocally take immediate steps to pass a third reconciliation bill in the event we lose the House, and stay as long as it takes to get it done,” a House GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Friday.

That strategy is likely to run into a brick wall, however, if Republicans are clobbered in the elections, and deflated GOP lawmakers lose their appetite to stick around Washington for too long afterwards, especially as the December holidays get closer. Those dynamics might be most pronounced in the House, where Republicans face the longest odds of keeping their majority, and attendance problems could undermine the party’s ability to move legislation.

“I envision a world where you get a lot of pressure from Trump and the White House to get more things across the finish line. … [But] I find it very hard to [see] them pass anything meaningful or significant. I just don’t think you’re going to have the enthusiasm of members to put up the fight and actually do all of that,” said a House GOP aide. “And, of course, if it’s a blowout, they’re not going to want to owe anything to Trump or the White House. They’re probably going to be blaming them. So they’re not going to want to help them out.”

Rep. Don Bacon (Neb.), a GOP centrist who’s retiring at the end of his term and has butted heads with Trump, said that he’s “skeptical that a new reconciliation bill will pass.”

“The president’s decisions to favor Russia after Congress overwhelmingly voted for sanctions have greatly reduced the president’s leverage. Why add funding to an agenda that we disagree with?” Bacon said.

Asked about whether he would stay during recess if Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) decides to push for a third reconciliation bill, Bacon merely said, “When the president is so wrong on Russia then he loses support.”

“Some folks are going to blame Trump on election results, and that will factor in,” he added.

Getting anything of substance done requires cooperation between chambers, and there are some Republicans in the Senate who also want to stay as long as possible in the event of an incoming Democratic majority.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) seemed confident earlier in October that a party-line reconciliation bill crammed with Republican wishes would get done in the lame duck if Congress was forced to stay in through New Year’s Eve.

“If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all,” Moreno told reporters at the Capitol on Oct. 15. “Like, we’ll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving because we have to get this done.”

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), who lost the South Carolina GOP gubernatorial primary, told The Hill that lawmakers were sent to Washington to “deliver results, not half-baked work.”

“Voters didn’t elect us to collect a paycheck and catch an early flight back home for recess,” Mace said. “If there’s work left to do, nobody should go home until it’s done.”

But Senate leaders are not as confident about that being a reality. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told The Washington Sun this week that while the election outcome could change senators’ attitudes about voting for reconciliation, he didn’t think any such package could pass at this point.

“Right now, we don’t have the votes to get on a third recon bill [and a] budget resolution. … We might have them after [the midterms],” Thune said. “We don’t have it now, and we don’t know that we have the votes to defend against the poison pill Democrat amendments.”

In order to make a reconciliation bill palatable (and possible) in the Senate, any additional spending in it has to be balanced by “pay-fors,” measures that raise revenue. A Senate Republican aide told The Hill that the existing House framework may not go over well with Senate fiscal hawks, and may not pass muster with Senate reconciliation “Byrd rules.”

“The conference just has so many different factions,” the aide said. “There are members that say we need pay-fors. The math for pay-fors that the House is doing is very creative … Do members believe that that is enough? That’s a question for them. And at this point, I just don’t think the answer is yes.”

There are also other priorities, especially if the Senate majority is changing hands, that will take up floor time before the holidays. Several administration nominees are still outstanding, including more than 30 that have gone through committee but need a floor vote. Those would have to start from zero in a new Congress regardless of who is in the majority, and Democrats are not likely to support Trump administration nominees.

The Senate Judiciary Committee was set to review and vote on a batch of judicial nominees on the last day before recess, but that meeting was canceled after a late-night vote. Those nominations are expected to come up in the lame duck as well.

And then there are other legislative moves: advancing a bipartisan permitting reform package is the first vote up on Nov. 9, when the Senate is scheduled to return. Like anything major in the Senate, that legislation will likely take weeks to get across the finish line.

Then there are regular bipartisan bills that re-up needed programs: the farm bill, an agriculture and food aid package and the National Defense Authorization Act, an annual defense policy bill. Congress also needs to fund the government by mid-December to prevent a shutdown.

That all stacks the odds against a reconciliation bill.

“I think reconciliation is more unlikely than not,” said a different Senate Republican aide.

But everyone admits the election result will change the calculus one way or another, and it’s hard to plan ahead without knowing it.

“We’re all focused on Tuesday,” said the second aide. “Of course, we know what needs to get done in a lame duck, and the Leader is going to assess the best play.”

articles.title: Vance road tests 2028 campaign as Trump’s midterm sideshow
articles.summary: Weatherton, TEXAS — Vice President Vance is homing in on his campaign message ahead of Election Day in what many see as a preview of a presidential bid in 2028 that seems all but certain. As Trump has criss-crossed the country for almost daily midterm rallies in the final month of campaigning, Vance’s schedule has…
articles.body:
Weatherton, TEXAS — Vice President Vance is homing in on his campaign message ahead of Election Day in what many see as a preview of a presidential bid in 2028 that seems all but certain.

As Trump has criss-crossed the country for almost daily midterm rallies in the final month of campaigning, Vance’s schedule has stayed just as busy — though his speeches and crowds are tight by comparison.

“He’s clearly sharpening his campaigning sword and building his IOU pile in preparation for a run,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor.

“Vance can’t draw Trump’s crowds, but he is energetic in his verbal knifing of Democrats,” he added.

That feistiness was on full display at a midterm rally in deep, red Weatherton, Texas on Thursday, where the crowd in a large construction warehouse was at capacity inside, with crowds watching on a jumbotron outside.

“I need you to tell James Talarico that this weird obsession with trans kids is not good for the state of Texas, and I need you to send the message to every far-left activist, to everybody who expects Texas to surrender, that in five days Texas is not surrendering a damn thing,” Vance said to an energized crowd, which at times chanted “JD!”

Vance, who authored “Hillbilly Elegy,” harkened back to his experience growing up in Appalachia, referring to himself as “a product of the American dream as your vice president.”

“Because the American dream was there for me, I want it to be there for you,” Vance told supporters in Texas.

Vance still invites plenty of criticism from his political adversaries over his messaging and delivery, as he tries to navigate the Trump 2.0 conundrum for Republicans: creating some distance from the president’s unpopular policies while building loyalty among his base.

During a Fox News town hall in Texas, the vice president was asked how young people can expect to get married and raise a family if homeownership is financially out of reach.

Before answering the question in full, Vance joked that he had only been asked one question about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s (R ) ass, alluding to one of Trump’s recent fixations.

Vance’s critics on the political left were quick to knock Vance’s initial response as cringey and out of touch.

The vice president also drew scorn from Democrats, and veered from some in his own party, when he spoke out in support of Vivek Ramaswamy’s divisive attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race, even as some in the GOP criticized their candidate.

Still, many Republicans are encouraged by his performance down the 2026 homestretch, ahead of what could be a bruising election for the party.

“He’s getting in some really good, quality political reps at that level right now, and taking advantage of the midterm calendar to do it while at the same time obviously going out to try and be helpful to candidates who need it in some really critical statewide races,” said one Republican strategist.

Vance has made stops in Kansas, Montana, North Carolina, and Texas this week alone. He’s given dozens of speeches since campaigning began for primaries, while also touring the country as the head of Trump’s fraud task force.

On Monday, he will return to his home state of Ohio to stump for Republicans in the contentious gubernatorial and Senate races. He’ll also campaign in Rome, N.Y., located in the state’s 21st congressional district. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the open race as “lean Republican.”

“I don’t know if it’s a test as much of an opportunity to show what he can do,” said Chris Johnson, an Ohio Republican strategist.

“I grew up with pretty center-right Ohio Republican politics and listening to JD talk radicalized me, and moved me toward this much more nationalist position,” he said.

While Vance has maintained he is laser-focused on the midterms, he regularly smiles off questions about his political future. And he said Trump would probably back him if he ran, in an interview with Mark Halperin on 2WAY earlier this month.

Although Trump has given Vance the fraud platform, the VP still faces the same hurdles as most VPs.

“When you’re in the role as vice president, you’re often limited to whatever the goals of the principal are,” Johnson said. “You’re also not really given a lot of wiggle room to do your own thing or have your own voice.”

“But he does have this really unique, compelling voice and story, and so when he’s been getting more leeway like he’s been getting recently to be himself, be authentic, that’s where you’re seeing the real success,” he continued.

The speculation around Vance, and other potential 2028 nominees, will hit fever pitch after the midterms.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, another contender for Trump’s crown, said last night that he has “no plans at this time” to run for president. Rubio has mostly steered clear of campaigning, but joined Trump on a trip to Texas earlier this week, speaking for about 11 seconds after Trump called him onto the stage.

Trump has not yet endorsed a candidate, but has described the prospect Vance and Rubio on the same ticket as the “dream team.”

“I think Vance probably gets first crack at it, you know the first opportunity, the first right of refusal,” the unnamed Republican strategist said.

But a bruising midterms could leave Republicans in disarray two years out from their post-Trump future.

“Any thought of ‘heir apparent’ is probably thrown out the window next Wednesday unless we defy gravity and beat the odd,” the strategist said.

“He’s going to have to work for it. He’s going to have to earn it,” the strategist added.

Vance has regularly topped straw polls in gatherings of hardcore Republican supporters. How that translates to primary elections will be tested in about 15 months.

“If the party faithful, starting with Iowa Caucus goers still want to continue the MAGA trend, then he is the likely nominee,” the unnamed strategist said.

Johnson noted that Vance’s age, 42, could work in his advantage, noting his popularity among young conservatives.

“If this leads to a sort of come-to-Jesus moment within the party, I think folks are going to immediately start looking forward, and if you’re looking forward, the immediate guy that you want to start thinking about is the vice president,” Johnson said.

articles.title: 2028 hopefuls with the most riding on the midterms
articles.summary: The candidates with the most at stake in Tuesday’s midterm elections won’t necessarily be the ones on the ballot. For a growing field of prospective 2028 presidential contenders in both parties, the results could offer an early test of their political strength, their influence within their respective parties and their ability to shape the next presidential race at a…
articles.body:
The candidates with the most at stake in Tuesday’s midterm elections won’t necessarily be the ones on the ballot.

For a growing field of prospective 2028 presidential contenders in both parties, the results could offer an early test of their political strength, their influence within their respective parties and their ability to shape the next presidential race at a time when both parties are looking to move away from the status quo.

From California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s restricting efforts to how the outcome impacts Vice President Vance’s chances, Tuesday’s returns could provide an early indication of which would-be White House hopefuls emerge stronger — and which face some vulnerabilities.

For Democrats, Michigan’s closely watched Senate race could provide a particularly consequential test for the party’s left flank and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who is considering a potential presidential bid or a run for a New York Senate seat.

A win by progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed over Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, would give Ocasio-Cortez a powerful argument that her brand of politics can prevail in a critical battleground state that Democrats will need in 2028.

Ocasio-Cortez has been selective about the candidates she campaigns for, making her decision to throw her support behind El-Sayed particularly significant. A win would not only underscore her political instincts but also inevitably boost her case for a White House bid.

“If El-Sayed can win there, AOC can win anywhere,” said Democratic strategist Brad Bannon, echoing the line that Ocasio-Cortez — or AOC as she is sometimes known — has been using in recent weeks to make the case that it could be her time.

“An El-Sayed victory in America’s great industrial heartland would prove an aggressive progressive like AOC could win the 2028 presidential election,” Bannon continued. “His win would be proof positive that voters nationally are sick and tired of business as usual.

“He and AOC represent a new kind of politics sweeping the nation and demonstrate the pressing need for fresh political faces,” Bannon added.

At the same time, if El-Sayed loses and a string of more moderate Democrats win, it could give an immediate shot in the arm to potential candidates like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.) and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.

“If El-Sayed loses, it will be a major exclamation point for moderates who have been saying, ‘Wake up guys, we can’t win national races with these folks,’” one major Democratic donor said. “And that means folks like Beshear and Kelly can start making that argument to the Democratic electorate in the next few months.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D), who is on the ballot unlike some of his potential White House contenders, would also benefit from a solid performance in his reelection campaign in Georgia.

While Democrats initially considered Ossoff to be in a tighter race, he is now expected to win against Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) on Tuesday. And while he has pledged to remain a senator for his entire term, the Democrats anticipate he might be drafted into a presidential campaign.

“A big night sets up the momentum for a potential run and the public perception around it. It’ll be a big deal,” said one prominent Democratic strategist.

Newsom also has some of his own political interests riding on Tuesday’s outcome.

If Democrats score sweeping victories — and double-digit gains in the House — he can claim credit for taking action with his redistricting efforts to help his party. Even a narrower victory could help bolster his presidential prospects if newly redrawn congressional districts in California help deliver a majority in the House.

But it could also hand Newsom evidence that his aggressive and confrontational tack with President Trump and other Republicans has been highly effective.

“Even if it’s a narrow win, he’s going to get a lot of credit and he can leverage that to show he did something,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist, who does not support Trump. “He can show he’s a fighter, not just a talker.”

For some Republicans, the stakes on Tuesday are just as high.

Vance could have the most on the line, depending on GOP performance in the elections. If Republicans get trounced in races across the country, it may cause Republicans to pivot from Trump and MAGA and create an immediate opening for other Republicans.

Major losses in both chambers would also put pressure on Vance to begin to move away from Trump, something he has been reluctant to do.

“It would definitely leave a vacuum in the Republican Party for new voices to come in,” Del Percio said. “Depending on how big the win for Democrats is, there are going to be some openings for Republicans.

“I think there are going to be a lot of voices speaking out because it will truly be the first time Donald Trump is a lame duck,” she added.

One former Trump campaign aide agreed that Vance is “in a really tough place” if the election goes sideways.

“If Tuesday goes poorly as expected, it’s going to make life even more difficult for him because how does he create any distance from Trump?” the former aide said. “He’s in a lose-lose situation.”

“Not only that but the only chance Republicans have of winning in 2028 is if Democrats nominate AOC or a Bernie-clone,” the GOP strategist said. “If the Democrats nominate a normie, the race is over, I can tell you that.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, often mentioned as a 2028 hopeful, could also be a victim of the fallout, Republicans say, but spared the brunt of it by the nonpolitical nature of his role.

Democratic strategist Fernand Amandi, who is consulting in two key Florida races including the gubernatorial race, said while the potential 2028 candidates have a lot riding on the midterms, “we’ve first got to see what the environment looks like when the smoke clears and that will begin on Wednesday morning.”

“But right now, it’s a jump ball,” Amandi said. ‘What makes this so interesting is that there is no clear cut person in the lead.”
