articles.title: The 10 races that will decide House control
articles.summary: The battle for the House majority will come down to a handful of battleground districts. Republicans are playing defense as they seek to defend their 218-214 majority while facing tough political headwinds. All 435 House seats are up for grabs. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner, rates 13 House contests as “toss ups.”…
articles.body:
The battle for the House majority will come down to a handful of battleground districts.

Republicans are playing defense as they seek to defend their 218-214 majority while facing tough political headwinds. All 435 House seats are up for grabs.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner, rates 13 House contests as “toss ups.” As of Friday, Democrats have an 82 percent chance of flipping the House.

Here are 10 of those key contests that will decide who wins control of the lower chamber:

Ohio’s 7th District has long been held by the GOP, but scandal-plagued Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) has put that streak in jeopardy.

Domestic abuse allegations against Miller from his ex-wife have rocked the race in northern Ohio. Emily Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), accused the House Republican of physical and emotional abuse, which Miller has denied .

He has faced calls to step aside from some Republicans — including Bernie Moreno .

Democrat Bryan Poindexter, a union iron worker and Brook Park City Council member, has run an aggressive campaign against Miller focused on economic issues and corruption, as well as his opponent’s abuse scandal.

Poindexter is narrowly favored to win and flip the seat for Democrats, DDHQ forecasts.

Rep. Ashley Hinson’s (R) open House seat in Iowa has become an unexpected battleground.

Favorable conditions for Democrats have made the seat, which Hinson won by more than 15 percentage points two years ago, increasingly competitive. DDHQ forecasts Democrat Lindsay James, a state lawmaker, the slight favorite to win the seat.

The Democrat has sought to tie her opponent, Joe Mitchell, to President Trump while also hammering the Republican over his residency . James has accused Mitchell of moving to the 2nd District to run for the open seat.

Mitchell, who is backed by the president, has campaigned on his opposition to special interests. He has called his opponent a radical leftist and criticized her over missing votes in the state Legislature.

A Democratic Tejano singer-songwriter may unseat a sitting member of Congress in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

Bobby Pulido is challenging Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas) for a seat she won by 14 points last cycle. The district, which runs through southern Texas, will serve as a key test of Latino voters’ appetite for Republicans this cycle. Trump made key gains with the bloc in 2024.

While GOP-led redistricting last year shifted the boundaries of De La Cruz’s district, she was seen as the favorite as the 2026 election cycle commenced. The incumbent still holds a slight upper hand, according to DDHQ.

Pulido has panned De La Cruz over her ties to Trump while the Republican has painted the singer as an out-of-touch celebrity. Both candidates have highlighted agriculture, border security and affordability issues as centerpieces of their campaigns.

The retirement of Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) put this classic swing district that has voted red in recent statewide elections back in play for the GOP.

DDHQ gives former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R) a slight edge in the contest.

The Republican is facing off against Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap in a tight contest that the GOP is looking to clinch. Cook Political Report shifted the race from “likely” to “leans” Republican in early October after a number of polls were released showing Dunlap in the lead.

Dunlap has zeroed in on the war in Iran and its effects on Mainers pocketbooks on the trail, while LePage has sought to paint his Democratic opponent as a radical.

This San Antonio-area district was redrawn to favor the GOP, but with the tides shifting among Latinos, that redistricting effort may not pay off.

Democratic Sheriff’s Deputy Johnny Garcia is running against Republican Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz for a seat held by Rep. Greg Casar (D), who is running in Texas’s 37th District under the new map. The Republican is slightly favored to win, DDHQ forecasts.

Cook Political Report moved the race from “leans Republican” to “toss up” in late October amid heavy super PAC spending from both parties. More than half of eligible voters in the district are Latinos, setting up another test of the GOP’s hold on the bloc.

Garcia describes himself as an “old school Democrat” running on lowering costs and ensuring public safety. Carlos De La Cruz, brother of Monica De La Cruz, is running on securing the border, fighting corruption, defeating the “woke left” and protecting farmers.

The district has seen a number of high-profile Republicans stump for Carlos De La Cruz. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has called the race the “ whole enchilada, ” and President Trump rallied with Carlos De La Cruz in San Antonio.

Both candidates have broken with their parties on the trail — Carlos De La Cruz called Trump’s tariffs “too broad,” and Garcia hit former President Biden over his handling of the southern border.

South Florida’s open 22nd District is home to a competitive race for a seat that Trump won by 10 points in 2024 but lost by 3 in 2020.

Democrat Pia Dandiya is facing Republican Casey Askar to represent the redrawn seat. Rep. Lois Frankel (D-Fla.) currently represents the district and is retiring after this term.

Askar is narrowly favored to win the seat, according to DDHQ , and high-profile figures , including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Johnson, have hit the trail in the Sunshine State.

Both candidates support a congressional stock trading ban. Dandiya, a former school principal, Apple lobbyist and White House Domestic Policy Council fellow, has campaigned on affordability, while Askar, a former Marine and CEO of a construction and real estate company, has underscored his alignment with the president.

This North Carolina seat won comfortably by Republicans two years ago may fall into the hands of Democrats after Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped out of the race.

Edwards called off his reelection bid following a rare censure from his House colleagues over allegations of sexual harassment from female staffers.

Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom took his place on the ballot and has been working to consolidate Republican support in a district with a 5-point GOP advantage , per the Cook Political Report Voter Index. Still, election handicappers have moved the race in Democrats’ direction, and DDHQ has Democrat Jamie Ager narrowly favored to win the seat in western North Carolina.

Ager, a fourth-generation farmer, has said his top priority if elected would be to deliver funds for Hurricane Helene recovery. His Republican opponent has also underscored her support for relief.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.) is in a tight race to hold his seat against Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti (D).

The first-term member of Congress won his race by less than 2 points in 2024. DDHQ forecasts that Cognetti is narrowly favored to win.

The Democrat has hit Bresnahan over his stock trading while in Congress, claiming he has made more than 600 trades worth $8 million. Bresnahan, meanwhile, has painted his opponent as a radical.

Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) is campaigning to hold his seat by touting his bipartisanship and ability to break with Trump.

He has touted his opposition to Trump’s tariffs on Canada and Republicans’ efforts to sell public lands.

Trump pulled his endorsement from Hurd after he pushed back on the president’s tariffs this spring, but he soon reversed and endorsed him for reelection after all. Hurd is the favorite heading into Tuesday, per DDHQ.

Combat veteran Dwayne Romero is challenging Hurd in the southwestern Colorado district that hasn’t elected a Democrat in nearly two decades.

Democrat Cait Conley, a combat veteran, is challenging Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) in a must-watch House race.

Lawler is one of two Republicans who won in districts former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024, demonstrating an ability to overcome tough odds in difficult climates. Still, Conely is the narrow favorite in DDHQ’s forecast.

The House Republican is seen as one of the most bipartisan members of Congress and carries large support within the Jewish community, a key constituency in his district. He has campaigned on tax relief, among other issues.

Conley, meanwhile, has focused on lowering the cost of healthcare and utility bills on the trail.

Democrats are eyeing a flip in the Big Sky State, with Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke opting to retire.

Although Republican Aaron Ford is narrowly favored to keep the seat in the GOP’s hands, per DDHQ’s forecast, Democrat Sam Forstag has picked up steam in the lead-up to Election Day.

A smokejumper and union leader, Forstag has zeroed in on working-class messaging throughout his campaign. He is notably backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

Flint, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, has Trump’s support. The president campaigned for the House hopeful earlier this month.

articles.title: A look inside the Somali mall where Omar reappeared after DC raid raises more failed assimilation concerns
articles.summary: Karmel Mall owner Basim Sabri gave a tour of the massive Somali mall in Minneapolis, raising questions about cultural assimilation in America.
articles.body: MINNEAPOLIS — The day after Rep. Ilhan Omar's first public appearance since the raid on her home, Fox News Digital was given a tour of the mall where she reemerged in her home state. The footage provides a glimpse inside an enclave within America that is dominated by Somalis and Somali culture, and a gives a peak into the community that Omar represents in the U.S. House of Representatives. The mall isn't just a place for people to buy clothing, food and receive services, but is a "community hub" of mostly women entrepreneurs, as described by a female shop owner. "We're here today are Karmel Mall with brother Basim, to kind of browse through this amazing community, corridor that is full of amazing women," she told Fox News Digital, referring the Karmel Mall of Somalia's owner, Basim Sabri, who provided the tour. 'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT Sabri, a Gaza-born immigrant, came to the United States to study in Minneapolis. During that time, he became a real-estate investor and steadily grew his business in the years to come. Now, he's a local titan of industry and owns a vast real estate empire, which includes the mall and several apartment complexes in the area that house Somalis. He has political ties at all levels of local and state politics, and is friends with Omar. He also knew the Somali-born congresswoman's father. Fox News Digital interviewed him separately, days before the official tour of the mall. For most inside, English is the mall's second language. It's packed with stores offering electronic SIM cards to call overseas, foreign money exchanges and travel agencies arranging trips to the Middle East and East Africa. Vendors also sell gold, fragrances and traditional Somali fashion items, mostly for women. There are Somali barber shops, cafes, traditional Somali food vendors and henna tattoo shops. Sabri gave conflicting figures on the exact number of stores, once saying 900, and later 750. SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME It sports a food court with a giant Somali flag painted on the ceiling, as well as Somali, Palestinian and American flags hanging from the walls. Many politicians use that space for press conferences, Sabri explained. It's also where Omar ate lunch with friends, supporters and state Attorney General Keith Ellison during Fox News Digital's foray into the mall when the lawmaker reemerged after casting an early ballot in her own reelection. Karmel Mall also has an Islamic weekend school for children, where they're taught the Quran and engage in recreational activities. While the mall isn't strictly for Somalis, few outside the Somali community were present when Fox News Digital toured. Fox News Digital was initially bucked by security upon attempting to enter and film inside the mall without Sabri's permission. The owner once banned Democratic Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey from the premises in February 2024 after he vetoed an Israel-Gaza ceasefire resolution passed by the City Council. OMAR’S MIDTERM RIVAL EXPOSES 'VICIOUS' SOMALI GANGS AMID IMMIGRATION PROBE INTO EMBATTLED REP "It is kind of an incubator setting where many businesses start in here, and then many succeed and grow and move somewhere else, to a bigger space," Sabri explained to Fox News Digital. He claims that the mall is a space where Somalis learn to integrate into the community. "You can see [the] Somalis not only integrating in the community, but also prospering," he said. "Somalis are very smart business individuals." But the mall's very name — the Karmel Mall of Somalia — along with the overwhelmingly Somali culture inside, raise questions about whether the group is actually assimilating into American society. WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH Steven Camerota is the director for research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). He pointed Fox News Digital to a CIS report published in December of last year that describes Somalis as a "struggling group." The report shows that more than half of children who live in the homes of Somali-born immigrants in Minnesota live in poverty, compared to only 8% of children living in homes of native-born Minnesotans. Among Somali-born immigrants who have lived in the United States for more than a decade, half cannot speak English "very well." The report says that 89% of Somali households receive some form of welfare, and 39% don't have high school diplomas, compared to only 8% of the native population. Camerota argued that across America, assimilation among various foreign-born groups, including Somalis, has dropped, though today's immigration numbers are about the same they were during America's first great wave of immigration. In the late 19th- and early 20th-centuries, immigrations from across the world flooded the United States. During that time, immigrants comprised about 15% of America's population, on par with todays numbers. After World War I, restrictive immigration policies that lasted until the 1960s took effect. In more recent history, immigration has ramped up to the tune of one million legal immigrants per year entering the United States, Camerota said. MINNESOTA SENATE HOPEFUL WARNS THREAT LEVEL RISING AMID RASH OF SOMALI GANG CRIME, TERROR PLOT "So, there are three big things about modern immigration that you can argue greatly hinder assimilation, and it has much less to do with the immigrants, and a lot more to do with just modern conditions," he told Fox News Digital. "The first is technology. You can fly home and visit home for the holidays if you want. In a way that just wouldn't have been possible in 1900, and in terms of costs." Camerota noted that the internet allows people access to constant news from home, and the constant ability to stay connected with family and friends via phone and video calls. "So this technology, travel and communications is fundamentally different today than in the past. And that likely means that the connection with the home country doesn't become as attenuated as quickly as it would have," he said. The attitudes of those who Camerota characterizes as "elites," in academia, government, media and other institutions has also changed. He said there are now dueling theories about the what exactly America is that could be contributing to a lack of assimilation. FORMER MN STATE TROOPER TEARS INTO DEMS AS SOMALI GANG VIOLENCE TERRORIZES MINNESOTA: ‘WHERE IS ILHAN OMAR?’ "So is America essentially a magnificent historical project of democracy and equality and republican government, or is it essentially — most of that's a sham and it's really a racist, sexist, homophobic [and] classist society?" he said. "The immigrants are arriving in a country in many ways that received both those messages, and so this elite attitude which permeates down is just so different than the world of the last great wave of immigration and almost certainly matters a great deal." Essentially, Camerota argued, if immigrants adopt the narrative that America is a fundamentally flawed nation, there is little reason for them to assimilate. "The word assimilation itself is seen as a bad word in many circles. The idea that immigrants are supposed to shed their their old culture and become American is now seen as a kind of for some — I don't want to say universally for all — but some fraction of it at least, as an undesirable Anglo conformity," he continued. "We are living in a country that can't really agree itself about its own history, let alone agree on what it wants from the immigrants." The third important fact to assimilation in Camerota's mind is the sheer number of immigrants coming to the United States. ALARMING FRAUD TREND PUTS SMALL-TOWN MOSQUE WITH INDUSTRY AND FOREIGN GOVT TIES IN FOCUS: ‘OUR MOTHERLAND NOW’ "The last point is numbers," he said. "So, we're at a record high now, right? 15% of the population is foreign born. It's matched the levels of between 1890 and 1910 ... during the last peak of the last great wave. But the one question then has to be asked, what happened then?" He said the immigration restriction of the mid 20th-century necessarily resulted in assimilation, as immigrants could not endlessly build enclaves for more and more foreign-born residents, as is happening today. "I think it's pretty clear it likely played a very big role in facilitating the assimilation of the immigrants," he said, suggesting that a similar immigration restriction could have the same effect if implemented now. Sabri has faced troubles of his own. In 2005, he was sentenced to 33 months in federal prison for bribing a local Minneapolis public official. He told Fox News Digital in the first interview about his time in prison, which included a brief stay at the infamous Federal Correctional Institution, Leavenworth in Kansas, in colorful detail. In that interview, he also insisted that the mall is for everyone. "But my experience is that Somalis are very, very intelligent and extremely hard-working people," he said. articles.title: Skilled trades now offer direct path to six-figure pay without college debt thanks to emerging tech industry
articles.summary: Andrew Miller says data center demand means electricians can earn six figures by age 22, with IBEW apprentices starting at $27 to $28 an hour.
articles.body: ASHBURN, Va. — Young Americans could be earning six-figure salaries without taking on college debt as the artificial intelligence boom fuels demand for skilled electricians, according to a veteran tradesman who says he has never struggled to find work in his 26-year career. Andrew Miller, who raised six children while working in the trades, said the rapid expansion of data centers is creating lucrative opportunities for young workers seeking financial independence without a traditional four-year college degree. "You don't have the debt that you incur in college," Miller told Fox News Digital inside one of Northern Virginia's largest data centers. He also explained the one of the reasons why Northern Virginia is one of the wealthiest enclaves in the U.S. is "directly linked to data centers and data center development." Miller claimed areas that reject the data center boom — like California — are seeing wealth leave the state. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING — AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED Miller said thanks to the explosion in the industry, electricians can earn six-figure salaries after completing their training, noting: "That is life changing to a 22, 23 year old individual." "They cannot produce enough electricians fast enough," he said. "I have never been without work in all my career even through recessions." While Miller acknowledged that the federal government's presence in Northern Virginia has historically helped sustain employment, he said the rapid expansion of data centers is expected to create even greater demand. "Now with data centers expanding it's going to just increase the demand for our trade," he said. Northern Virginia has earned the nickname "Data Center Alley" for its massive concentration of data centers, with Loudoun County at the heart of the nation's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure. As of March 2026, more than 230 data centers had been built or were under construction in the county, with another 116 projects in the pipeline. INSIDE THE NEIGHBORHOOD LIVING ON THE EDGE OF AMERICA’S TECH FRONTIER Bill McGraw of electrical contractor J.E. Richards said apprenticeship programs offer an alternative to traditional college degrees, allowing participants to receive classroom instruction while gaining paid, hands-on experience. McGraw said apprentices accepted into a program through International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26 can start at approximately $27 to $28 an hour, even without previous experience. At the journeyman level, McGraw cited wages of approximately $62 an hour, equivalent to nearly $129,000 annually based on a 40-hour workweek year-round, before overtime. Don Slaiman said Local 26's hiring hall has grown from fewer than 9,000 workers to more than 17,500 amid Northern Virginia's data center boom. IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE'S WHAT WE SAW The demand extends beyond construction, with electricians needed for ongoing maintenance, equipment upgrades and infrastructure improvements. "There's always continuous work there," McGraw said. The economic benefits also reach surrounding communities. Miller said a single data center construction project can employ as many as 2,000 craft workers, generating business for local restaurants, housing providers and other services. "Those craft workers are gonna need a place to eat, sleep. They're gonna live in the community," Miller said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With artificial intelligence accelerating demand for new facilities, Slaiman said the growing industry offers workers a path to financial stability and opportunities to support their families. "We're going to need more data centers and we're going to build them and we are going to give great careers to folks," Slaiman said, adding that those jobs can help workers "raise a family and live the American dream."

articles.title: JOHN NAGEL: Ilhan Omar, my opponent, had a choice and picked political theater
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar shared a stage with far-left streamer Hasan Piker despite urgent warnings from Sen. Amy Klobuchar, Mayor Jacob Frey, and the Jewish Community Relations Council.
articles.body: Days before an election, with Minnesotans voting on crime, prices and the future of their neighborhoods, Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar had to decide who she would stand beside. She chose the far-left streamer, Hasan Piker. This is a man who said "America deserved 9/11." He called Hamas "a thousand times better" than Israel and said he would vote for Hamas "every single time." He called Orthodox Jews "inbred," waved off Hamas’s treatment of women and gay people as domestic policy he doesn’t care about, and warned this summer that if American Jews keep supporting Israel, someone "is going to come around and take action." Omar knew all of it. Everyone did. LEFTIST STREAMER TRIGGERS FURY AFTER MOCKING 'FUNNY' INJURIES TO ICE AGENTS AT ILHAN OMAR EVENT: ‘DISGUSTING’ Before Monday night, when she appeared for a live conversation and Q&A event in Minneapolis titled "I'm the Host Now!", the Jewish Community Relations Council of Minnesota and the Dakotas called her decision to participate "a betrayal of Jewish Minnesotans." Her district includes St. Louis Park, long the center of Jewish life in this state. Her own party’s Jewish caucus said Piker’s brand of hate has no place in Minnesota. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, called his statements reckless and unacceptable. Rep. Angie Craig, Rep. Betty McCollum, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, and state Sen. Ron Latz all spoke out. Democratic leaders privately urged her to cancel. Omar’s answer? Her campaign said the Democratic Party is a "big tent" — and she walked out on stage on Oct. 26, anyway. Ilhan Omar has had years to show Minnesota what kind of representative she is. Last Monday, she answered the question herself. Once there, Piker called Republicans "terrorists." Omar called the GOP the "pedophile protection party." ILHAN OMAR'S RADICAL STREAMER ALLY RALLIES WITH EMBATTLED LAWMAKER AFTER DC HOME RAID Let’s be clear about what this was. Not an old clip dug up by an opposition researcher. Not a careless remark from a decade ago. It was a deliberate decision, made over the objections of her own party and her own Jewish constituents, at an event built to turn out votes, hosted by state Sen. Omar Fateh, a member of the Twin Cities Democratic Socialists of America. Rep. Omar didn’t stumble into this. She calculated that a sold-out crowd was worth more than the trust of the Jewish families she represents. That isn’t a lapse in judgment. It is her judgment. And it fits. This is a congresswoman who has already had to apologize for trafficking in antisemitic tropes, who treats half the country as an enemy and calls it courage. WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS I spent 30 years with the Minnesota State Patrol. In law enforcement, you learn that character shows in what someone does after they’ve been warned: whom they trust, what they tolerate, whether they change course or double down. Omar was warned. She doubled down. Minnesota’s Fifth District deserves better. The district is home to families worried about violent crime, grocery bills, rent and whether their kids will have the opportunities they did. It is also home to immigrants who came here because they believe in America and to Jewish Minnesotans who should never have to wonder whether their own congresswoman takes threats against them seriously. SEE IT: TOP DEM OPERATIVE DRAWS LINE AT ‘DEPLORABLE’ HASAN PIKER AFTER TOUTING PARTY’S ‘BIG TENT’ During my time with the State Patrol, I never asked anyone’s party before responding to a crash. Public service means serving everyone — including the people who didn’t vote for you. I’m a Republican, and I won’t pretend otherwise. I believe the border must remain secure, violent criminals and fraudsters must be held accountable, families need relief from the cost of living, and police officers deserve support, not contempt. I believe America is worth defending. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But I don’t believe the people who disagree with me are terrorists. You can fight hard for your principles without calling millions of your fellow citizens enemies — and without sharing a microphone with a man who says his country deserved to be attacked. Ilhan Omar has had years to show Minnesota what kind of representative she is. Last Monday, she answered the question herself. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Now voters get to answer it. We can choose public safety over political theater, accountability over excuses, and respect for our neighbors over endless division. Ilhan Omar made her choice. On Nov. 3, the Fifth District gets to make ours.

articles.title: Trump makes war on the International Criminal Court
articles.summary: “It is only a matter of time” before the International Criminal Court interferes with “American military and law enforcement operations,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned in July. Convinced that such meddling would “mean the death of the United States as a sovereign and independent nation,” Rubio promised that the U.S. would use “all the…
articles.body:
“It is only a matter of time” before the International Criminal Court interferes with “American military and law enforcement operations,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned in July. Convinced that such meddling would “mean the death of the United States as a sovereign and independent nation,” Rubio promised that the U.S. would use “all the tools” at its disposal to “dismantle” the court, “brick by brick.”

On Oct. 9, the Trump administration, which had previously sanctioned 17 of the court’s judges, prosecutors and officials , froze its U.S. assets and prohibited Americans and American companies, with limited exceptions, from doing business with it. The goal, said Rubio , is to starve “this rogue court” of resources and cripple “its ability to operate.”

The International Criminal Court, it is worth noting, was established to prosecute perpetrators of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In an era marked by “might makes right,” it provides a forum for trying offenders when national legal systems cannot or will not. It also encourages governments to conduct their own trials and helps strengthen international norms.

To be sure, the court can in theory prosecute Americans for crimes committed in countries that have accepted its jurisdiction. But multiple obstacles make such prosecutions unlikely.

Since beginning operations nearly a quarter of a century ago, the court has convicted only 15 defendants , none of them Americans.

The International Criminal Court can only prosecute someone if the relevant national legal system is unable or unwilling to do so. Moreover, the court has no police force — it depends entirely on member states to execute its arrest warrants.

But even countries legally obligated to cooperate with the court may refuse to surrender politically powerful defendants. For example, in 2023, the court issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin for war crimes in Ukraine. In 2024, Putin visited Mongolia, an ICC member state. He was welcomed , not arrested.

Last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Hungary, another ICC member, despite a 2024 arrest warrant relating to the war in Gaza. Hungarian officials welcomed him as well.

In the early 2000s, the U.S. threatened to withhold military assistance and foreign aid from governments that refused to enter into treaties designed to prevent them from surrendering Americans to the International Criminal Court without U.S. consent. More than 100 countries ultimately signed. The U.S. also uses status of forces agreements to protect military personnel stationed abroad.

That said, the court still has an impact that the Trump administration doesn’t like. Even though Putin and Netanyahu remain in power, the court’s arrest warrants undermine their legitimacy, limit their travel, and brand some of their actions as not just illegitimate but criminal.

And in 2020, the court authorized an investigation into alleged atrocities in Afghanistan, including possible crimes by U.S. soldiers and Central Intelligence Agency personnel. In the face of intense political pressure , including the threat of sanctions against court personnel, the prosecutor ultimately focused his investigation on crimes committed by the Taliban and ISIS-K.

But even though no American has yet been charged, let alone tried, the Trump administration views the mere possibility of an investigation as intolerable.

President Trump is not alone in regarding the court as a grave threat to U.S. sovereignty. In 2002, President George W. Bush took the unprecedented step of rescinding former President Bill Clinton’s signature on the treaty establishing the International Criminal Court. That same year, the Republican-dominated Congress enacted the American Service-members’ Protection Act , sometimes called the “Hague Invasion Act,” authorizing the use of all necessary means — including military force — to free American or allied personnel detained by the court.

In contrast, former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden cooperated selectively with court investigations and arrests. Obama supported the Security Council’s decision to refer atrocities in Libya to the court. Biden lifted sanctions that had been imposed in Trump’s first term. But neither administration accepted the court’s jurisdiction over Americans, and Biden strongly opposed the arrest warrant against Netanyahu.

What distinguishes Trump’s approach is his determination to punish the court in ways that go far beyond inhibiting the prosecution of Americans. his tactics have infuriated many of America’s closest allies, most of which are among the 125 states that have ratified the court’s statute. They have denounced U.S. sanctions and pledged “to support the court’s vital work.” European governments may even invoke the EU blocking statute to prevent their companies from complying with U.S. sanctions.

Why would the U.S. risk such a confrontation over an institution that poses so little danger to American interests? The answer lies in a worldview that resists any constraints on American power. Trump’s National Security Strategy insists on unilateral action to advance U.S. economic and security interests. Eager to escape the “sovereignty-sapping incursions” of international organizations, Trump has ordered U.S. withdrawal from 66 of them.

Nonetheless, the Oct. 9 sanctions break new ground. Instead of simply refusing to participate in an international institution it dislikes, the administration aims to put the International Criminal Court out of business.

In the name of defending American sovereignty, Trump seeks to deny other sovereigns the right to rely on an institution they created to pursue accountability for the worst international crimes. That irony is not lost on the rest of the world.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.standfirst: El economista pone en duda las palabras del ministro sobre la fiabilidad de las vías
articles.summary: El economista pone en duda las palabras del ministro sobre la fiabilidad de las vías
articles.body: Continúa la polémica en torno al accidente ferroviario de Urda, Toledo, que ha dejado, por el momento, 69 muertos. Ahora, en una última rueda de prensa, el ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, explicó que el sistema de seguridad LZB que se usa en esa vía había sufrido 170 fallos en lo que llevamos de 2026. Eso sí, quiso dejar claro que el 75% de los fallos no eran propios del sistema, si no que se habían producido por algo externo, como robos de cable de cobre o las condiciones meteorológicas, lo que acaba dañando a estructura. De las 170 incidencias reportadas, 13 de ellas se produjeron en el tramo de vía de Urda. Esto le ha sorprendido mucho al economista Gonzalo Bernardos, cuestionándose por qué no se ha tenido en cuenta esto antes: “Si Óscar Puente valora cerrar durante dos años la línea de alta velocidad Barcelona - Madrid es porque no cree que sea lo suficientemente segura. Entonces, ¿lo era hace unos días? En concreto, ¿antes del accidente de Urda? Impresionante”. En esa conferencia de prensa, Puente señaló: “No le oculto que esta es ahora mismo una de las cosas que estamos valorando, pero no solo por una cuestión de seguridad, sino por múltiples razones. España y Alemania en esto son dos países que funcionan de una manera completamente distinta. Este sistema no lo he establecido yo, es un sistema en el que se viene trabajando tradicionalmente”. Pasando a explicar cómo funciona cada país: “En Alemania, en casi todas las ocasiones, cuando hay que afrontar una renovación de línea se corta el servicio y se procede a renovar la línea de manera completa, privando del servicio a los usuarios durante el tiempo en el que esas obras tienen lugar”. “Nuestro sistema es el opuesto, es decir, en España se prima la prestación del servicio a la realización de las obras, es decir, se supedita la realización de las obras a la prestación del servicio, con las consecuencias de que la fiabilidad y la puntualidad, sin duda, se ven afectadas”, mantuvo. Dejando claro que cerrar la línea Madrid-Barcelona es una posibilidad: “Tardaríamos mucho menos tiempo, estaríamos hablando de que una obra que igual nos puede llevar cinco años en banda de mantenimiento, podríamos dejarla reducida a menos de 24 meses o 12 meses, en condiciones normales, pero durante ese tiempo privar del servicio a los usuarios”, sentenció.

articles.title: Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed v Mike Rogers
articles.summary: Al Jazeera examines the crucial US Senate race in Michigan, including candidate positions and largest spenders.
articles.body:
Dearborn, Michigan – Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who has been volunteering to help elect Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, says he’s spoken in recent days to journalists from Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom.

The United States Senate race between El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers is attracting national and international attention, reflecting the potent political symbolism that belies its outcome, which extends far beyond one seat in the upper chamber of Congress.

Supporters in each camp paint the contest as a crucial fight that could shape the political direction of the state and the nation for years.

Abdulrazek, a small business owner, said the election is a chance to hold Trump accountable for breaking his promises to pursue peace in the world and focus on the needs of Americans.

For Arab and Muslim communities that have been facing Islamophobic attacks as part of the Senate race, the vote is pivotal, he added.

“What’s on the line is they have to stand up for themselves and say, ‘We are part of this country, and we’re going to be voting, and we will actually make a change’,” Abdulrazek told Al Jazeera.

Here, Al Jazeera looks at the US Senate race in Michigan and why it has gained so much attention.

El-Sayed is a public health advocate who previously led the health department in Detroit and Wayne County in southeast Michigan. He is 42.

If elected, the Democrat of Egyptian descent would become the first-ever Muslim US senator.

El-Sayed ran for governor in 2018 but fell short in the Democratic primary against eventual winner Gretchen Whitmer. The Democratic nominee has embraced progressive policies, especially Medicare for All – a plan to expand government-funded healthcare to everyone in the US.

Rogers is a 63-year-old former US Congress member and state legislator. The Republican nominee ran for the Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost to centrist Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin.

He is a close ally of Donald Trump, but has sought to create some distance between his campaign and the unpopular president.

For example, Rogers has supported Trump’s decision to join Israel in launching the war against Iran, while also calling for an end to the conflict.

The Republican candidate also backs tax cuts, increasing domestic energy production and deregulation.

It will be difficult for Democrats to gain control of the Senate if they lose Michigan. The seat is currently held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters.

A Rogers win would hand the swing state Senate seat to Republicans for at least six years.

The race, however, is not just about the partisan math in the Senate. It is a test of the electoral viability of progressive ideas, including sharp criticism of Israel, in a swing state.

While the Senate has many progressive members, most come from coastal states considered Democratic strongholds.

A victory for El-Sayed in Michigan would show that his message can attract a winning coalition, which could influence how Democratic presidential candidates may go about their campaigning in 2028.

There is also the factor of El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, which had become the subject of near daily attacks by Rogers and Trump.

The race has raised questions about whether Michigan and the US are ready for a Muslim senator.

Why has Israel become a major issue in the race?

El-Sayed has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza, echoing the findings of major human rights organisations and United Nations investigators.

The Democrat has also linked wars, including the conflict in Iran and US aid to Israel, to domestic issues. He says that US taxpayer money is better spent on addressing issues at home, such as healthcare and crumbling infrastructure. Pro-Israel groups, namely the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), have spent tens of millions of dollars to help defeat El-Sayed.

AIPAC backed El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens with more than $30m, making Israel policy one of the most discussed subjects in the election.

El-Sayed overcame the spending onslaught in the primaries, but Rogers – a staunch Israel supporter – has seized on the criticism of El-Sayed from pro-Israel advocates, including some Democrats.

Rogers – who has pledged unconditional support for Israel – has accused El-Sayed of caring more for Palestine than Michigan.

After a lull in spending in Michigan, AIPAC has returned to the race to back Rogers.

The pro-Israel lobby group’s election arm, United Democracy Project, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on mailers against El-Sayed. According to The New York Times, it has funnelled $9m to a Republican group supporting Rogers.

Why is Haley Stevens back in the headlines?

It is uncommon for the candidate who lost a primary to be part of a major storyline in the general election, but Stevens has been making headlines days ahead of the vote after her fiance endorsed Rogers, citing El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Stevens, a Democrat in the US House of Representatives, has also criticised El-Sayed for his positions on Israel while saying she would still vote for the Democratic candidate.

The congresswoman’s repeated media appearances bashing El-Sayed have earned the scorn of some Democrats.

On Friday, El-Sayed and several Democratic-aligned groups and politicians responded to Stevens, saying that the party must focus on winning the Senate seat.

El-Sayed said in a statement that while “defeating Trump’s hand-picked candidate” should be the priority, “Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”

Both Rogers and El-Sayed supporters interviewed by Al Jazeera have stressed the race’s importance.

Former Democratic Cynthia Johnson said the negative campaigning around El-Sayed’s religion and ethnicity makes the election especially crucial.

“What’s really at stake is life or death. Our children are being exposed to some very negative, nasty things,” Johnson told Al Jazeera.

“We have to vote like our lives depended on it because we have a person who’s in the White House right now who’s a maniac and we need as many people who are going to speak up as possible – people like Abdul.”

Outside a Trump rally on Sunday, Rogers supporter Rob Cortis expressed similar urgency.

“This election is so important. Our country is at stake. Our border is at stake. The future of our children in America is at stake,” Cortis told Al Jazeera.

“If it flips to communism, socialism or if it goes to Muslim rule America was never intended for that. America is intended to be a nation of Christians, showing the goodness of God.”

Most recent polls have shown El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers – ranging from four to seven percentage points.

However, polling in Michigan – a diverse state of more than 10 million people – has been unreliable over the past decades, often getting the results wrong by several percentage points.

The Cook Political Report has classified the race as a toss-up and both campaigns have warned their supporters that the result may come down to a few thousand votes.

With nearly $300m spent, Michigan’s Senate race is quickly becoming one of the most expensive in the country.

Political action committees (PACs) aligned with both major parties have been buying ads in support of their respective candidates.

On the Republican side, one of the largest spenders has been Senate Leadership Fund, whose largest donors include pro-Israel billionaire Miriam Adelson.

MAGA Inc and its subsidiary No Going Back, a pro-Trump group funded by the US president’s allies, including Adelson and Elon Musk, have also spent millions of dollars on the race.

Great Lakes Conservatives Fund (GLCF), a Michigan Republican PAC that AIPAC has backed in general elections, has also been a big spender, according to media reports.

The Senate Majority PAC (SMP) and an affiliated group called WINSENATE have been the largest spenders. SMP’s top funders include businessmen Eychaner Fred and Amos Hostetter Jr.

Early voting is underway across Michigan and hundreds of thousands of people have already cast their ballots.

Election day, Tuesday, November 3, will be the last day to vote. Polls in Michigan close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday).

That depends on how close the race is. If it’s a tight contest, Michigan likely will not find out who won until Wednesday. In the primaries in August, when El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens, the Associated Press did not call the race until about 10am (15GMT) on the Wednesday after election day.

Likewise, Michigan was called for Trump in 2024 around 1pm (18:00 GMT) on the day after the election.

However, if one of the candidates acquires a commanding lead across the state, he could be projected as the winner hours after the polls close.

articles.title: Comer says there’s a ‘big possibility’ Peltola won’t be seated if she wins
articles.summary: Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said there is a “big possibility” that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) won’t be seated even if she wins Alaska’s Senate race following reports that her campaign participated in a “ballot-stacking” scheme. Appearing on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning,” Comer was asked if there was a possibility Peltola would not be seated…
articles.body:
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said there is a “big possibility” that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) won’t be seated even if she wins Alaska’s Senate race following reports that her campaign participated in a “ ballot-stacking ” scheme.

Appearing on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning,” Comer was asked if there was a possibility Peltola would not be seated even if she won the election.

“That’s a big possibility. I have not spoken to Senator Thune about that. We kind of tend to operate within the confinement of the House with respect to our investigations, but at the end of the day, I think the American people can see loud and clear what was done here,” Comer, the House Oversight Committee chair, said.

Comer, particularly, has heavily criticized Peltola’s campaign over a New York Times report that alleged her campaign and national Democrats recruited another candidate who shared the same name as her Republican opponent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in order to dilute the GOP vote.

Ballot “stacking” is a common practice, especially in Alaska’s unusual nonpartisan, top four voting system. GOP strategists previously told The Hill that it is not illegal.

“We cannot allow this to happen. And the fact that there are a lot of people involved in the Democrat National Party who have been silent on this, and the question remains: Who all was involved? When did this involvement begin? Did money change hands? That’s a big question,” Comer continued. “That’s probably the biggest question that needs to be answered. Did money change hands? And then you know what laws were broken after that?”

He has already launched a probe into Peltola’s involvement in the operation – scheduling transcribed interviews for both Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who The Times spoke with, and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic operative, requesting in-person, transcribed interviews.

Comer requested that Rios testify on Nov. 5 and Kurtz on Nov. 6.

Sullivan said earlier Sunday that he would accept the election results even if he lost though Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) dodged answering the same question.

articles.title: Stevens staff resign over Rogers endorsement
articles.summary: Staffers for Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) are reportedly resigning over the lawmaker’s recent decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s competitive Senate race. “Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens,” the automated email reply from Stevens’s former communications director reads. A statement, first…
articles.body:
Staffers for Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) are reportedly resigning over the lawmaker’s recent decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s competitive Senate race.

“Hello, as of November 1st I am no longer with the Office of Congresswoman Haley Stevens,” the automated email reply from Stevens’s former communications director reads.

A statement , first shared by CNN, from Stevens longtime chief of staff Justin German said as of Sunday morning, “Many members of our team have resigned, including myself.”

“We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’s decision to support Mike Rogers,” German wrote.

German — who worked with Stevens for 8 years — encouraged “everyone to exercise their civic duty, vote for Abdul and Democrats up and down the ballot, and stand up for the America we all believe in.”

Before her endorsement, Stevens was slated to appear alongside Democrat Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, but the Democratic nominee dropped Stevens from the campaign event, according to sources familiar with the matter.

When asked about her decision to endorse Rogers, Stevens said in a press conference it was in response to “hate” and El-Sayed’s ties to political streamer Hasan Piker.

“It’s my personal and private decision. I still love the party. I’ve done a ton for the party. I’ve voted for the party over and over and over again. I’m going to continue to do that as I fill out my term,” the lawmaker said.
